Another file may not use it. This is the `private` that Go has no word for, checked at build time.\n22\t\n23\t## Why\n24\t\n25\tGo has two levels of visibility, and the lower one covers the whole package.\n26\t\n27\t| Level | Reach |\n28\t| --- | --- |\n29\t| Exported | Every importer |\n30\t| Unexported | **Every file in the package** |\n31\t\n32\tThere is no third level. In a flat package, every helper is a package-wide name, and every field is a package-wide reach.\n33\t\n34\tSplitting the package to get a boundary has a price.\n35\t\n36\t- Import cycles, and interfaces written only to break them.\n37\t- **Every name the two halves share has to be exported.** You wanted a boundary between two files, and you published an API.\n38\t- **A wrong boundary costs more.** Moving a declaration between files is free. Moving it between packages breaks every importer.\n39\t\n40\t`internal/` does not help here. It limits who may import a package, but it adds no level below unexported. So most Go code is better off flat, and the cost appears inside the package.\n41\t\n42\tTeams handle this with a convention: *this helper belongs to this file.* The convention lives only in the heads of the people who wrote the package.\n43\t\n44\tAn AI agent does not know it either. It sees an unexported helper in scope, so it calls it. It sees an unexported field, so it writes to it. Each edit compiles and passes a quick review, and the package becomes a mesh.\n45\t\n46\tdeclscope checks the convention instead. When an agent crosses a boundary, it is told what it crossed and given a fix. The decision is then written in the source, where the next agent reads it.\n47\t\n48\t### What it reports\n49\t\n50\tOne `database` package holds a repository per entity.\n51\t\n52\t```go\n53\t// user_repository.go\n54\tpackage database\n55\t\n56\timport (\n57\t\t\"context\"\n58\t\t\"database/sql\"\n59\t\t\"strings\"\n60\t\n61\t\t\"example.com/app/domain\"\n62\t)\n63\t\n64\ttype UserRepository struct{ db *sql.DB }\n65\t\n66\tfunc (r *UserRepository) Find(ctx context.Context, id int64) (*domain.User, error) {\n67\t\trow := r.db.QueryRowContext(ctx, `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = ?`, id)\n68\t\treturn scanUser(row)\n69\t}\n70\t\n71\tfunc scanUser(row *sql.Row) (*domain.User, error) {\n72\t\tvar u domain.User\n73\t\tvar email string\n74\t\tif err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &email); err != nil {\n75\t\t\treturn nil, err\n76\t\t}\n77\t\tu.Email = normalizeEmail(email)\n78\t\treturn &u, nil\n79\t}\n80\t\n81\tfunc normalizeEmail(s string) string {\n82\t\treturn strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s))\n83\t}\n84\t```\n85\t```go\n86\t// order_repository.go\n87\tpackage database\n88\t\n89\timport (\n90\t\t\"database/sql\"\n91\t\n92\t\t\"example.com/app/domain\"\n93\t)\n94\t\n95\ttype OrderRepository struct{ db *sql.DB }\n96\t\n97\tfunc scanOrder(rows *sql.Rows) (domain.Order, error) {\n98\t\tvar o domain.Order\n99\t\tvar email string\n100\t\tif err := rows.Scan(&o.ID, &email); err != nil {\n101\t\t\treturn domain.Order{}, err\n102\t\t}\n103\t\to.BuyerEmail = normalizeEmail(email)\n104\t\treturn o, nil\n105\t}\n106\t```\n107\t\n108\tThe two scan helpers are named apart by hand, since only one could be called `scan`. That mark says which repository owns which helper, and nothing holds anyone to it.\n109\t\n110\t`normalizeEmail` was written for `scanUser`. `scanOrder` calls it, and the compiler accepts that.\n111\t\n112\t```console\n113\t$ declscope ./...\n114\tuser_repository.go:28:6: func normalizeEmail is private to namespace \"userRepository\", but is used from namespace \"orderRepository\"\n115\torder_repository.go:17:17: \tused here, in namespace \"orderRepository\"\n116\t```\n117\t\n118\tA crossing has two answers.\n119\t\n120\t| Answer | How |\n121\t| --- | --- |\n122\t| Keep the boundary | Move the call inside the namespace |\n123\t| Share on purpose | Write `//declscope:shared`, which `-fix` inserts |\n124\t\n125\tHere the helper belongs to neither repository. The repair is a third file, and a stated scope.\n126\t\n127\t```go\n128\t// email.go\n129\tpackage database\n130\t\n131\timport \"strings\"\n132\t\n133\t//declscope:shared\n134\tfunc normalizeEmail(s string) string {\n135\t\treturn strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s))\n136\t}\n137\t```\n138\t\n139\t> [!TIP]\n140\t> `-fix` always widens, because that is the repair a tool can apply. It writes the directive where the declaration stands, and never moves a declaration to another file. Where the boundary is worth keeping, move the call yourself.\n141\t\n142\t### Where declscope sits\n143\t\n144\tThree linters draw boundaries in Go, at three scales.\n145\t\n146\t![A Go program drawn as nested frames. Between the api and database packages, depguard asks whether one package may import another. A green arrow runs from api to database, and a red one back from database to api is crossed out. Inside database, between user_repository.go and order_repository.go, declscope asks whether one file may reach another's declaration. A red arrow from scanOrder to normalizeEmail is crossed out. At the edge of the program, deadcode asks whether anything is reachable at all. The mail package sits greyed out with no arrow entering it, captioned unreachable.](docs/boundaries.png)\n147\t\n148\t| Linter | Scale | The question it answers |\n149\t| --- | --- | --- |\n150\t| [`depguard`](https://github.com/OpenPeeDeeP/depguard) | Between packages | May this package import that one? |\n151\t| **declscope** | Within one package | May this file reach that declaration? |\n152\t| [`deadcode`](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode) | Whole program | Is this reachable at all? |\n153\t\n154\tThe three compose. `depguard` keeps the package graph honest, declscope keeps each package honest inside, and `deadcode` removes what neither needs to reach.\n155\t\n156\t## Install\n157\t\n158\t| Method | Command | Needs |\n159\t| --- | --- | --- |\n160\t| **[mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/)** *(recommended)* | `mise use \"github:mpyw/declscope@0.24.1\"` | Nothing. Installs the prebuilt binary |\n161\t| `go tool` | `go get -tool github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest` | Go 1.27+ |\n162\t| `go install` | `go install github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest` | Go 1.27+ |\n163\t| Release archive | See below | Nothing |\n164\t\n165\t```bash\n166\tdeclscope ./...\n167\t```\n168\t\n169\t<details>\n170\t<summary>Pin a version, run through <code>go vet</code>, or install from an archive</summary>\n171\t\n172\t`mise use` pins the version in the project's `mise.toml`, so every checkout and CI run the same one. Add `-g` to install it for every project on your machine instead.\n173\t\n174\t```toml\n175\t[tools]\n176\t\"github:mpyw/declscope\" = \"0.24.1\"\n177\t```\n178\t\n179\tAs a tool dependency in `go.mod`:\n180\t\n181\t```bash\n182\tgo get -tool github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest\n183\tgo tool declscope ./...\n184\t```\n185\t\n186\tThrough `go vet`, which runs it with the same package loading as the rest of your vet checks:\n187\t\n188\t```bash\n189\tgo vet -vettool=$(which declscope) ./...\n190\t```\n191\t\n192\t> [!WARNING]\n193\t> **`go vet` does not see changes to config or baseline files.** It caches the result of each package, and the cache key does not include these files. After a change to either one, run `go vet` once with **`-a`**:\n194\t>\n195\t> ```bash\n196\t> go vet -a -vettool=$(which declscope) ./...\n197\t> ```\n198\t>\n199\t> Without `-a`, `go vet` can report the result of the old configuration. New diagnostics can be missing, and old ones can remain. Running `declscope` directly is not affected.\n200\t\n201\tWithout installing anything:\n202\t\n203\t```bash\n204\tgo run github.com/mpyw/declscope/cmd/declscope@latest ./...\n205\t```\n206\t\n207\tFrom a release archive, verified against the published checksums:\n208\t\n209\t```bash\n210\tVERSION=0.24.1\n211\tcurl -LO \"https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/releases/download/v${VERSION}/declscope_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz\"\n212\tcurl -LO \"https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/releases/download/v${VERSION}/checksums.txt\"\n213\tshasum -a 256 -c checksums.txt --ignore-missing\n214\ttar xzf \"declscope_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz\"\n215\t```\n216\t\n217\t</details>\n218\t\n219\t### Flags\n220\t\n221\t| Flag | Default | Effect |\n222\t| --- | --- | --- |\n223\t| `-config` | *(discovered)* | Path to a YAML config file. Skips the [`.declscope.yaml` lookup](#configuration) |\n224\t| `-test` | `true` | Analyze `*_test.go` files as well |\n225\t| `-fix` | `false` | Apply suggested fixes |\n226\t| `-diff` | `false` | With `-fix`, print a diff instead of writing files |\n227\t| `-V=full` | | Print the version and exit. `go run`, or a build with `-buildvcs=false`, answers `devel` |\n228\t\n229\t`-test`, `-fix` and `-diff` come from `go/analysis`. `declscope -help` lists the rest.\n230\t\n231\t### Subcommands\n232\t\n233\t| Command | What it does | Flags of its own |\n234\t| --- | --- | --- |\n235\t| `declscope survey [packages]` | [Report what was checked and what it found](#measuring-what-is-there), one row per package | `-format`, `-test`, `-config`, `-allow-errors` |\n236\t| `declscope inspect <package>` | [Report the shape of one package](#measuring-what-is-there): its namespaces and the crossings between them | `-format`, `-test`, `-config` |\n237\t| `declscope baseline [packages]` | [Record the violations a codebase already has](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase), `shrink`'s included | `-config`, `-o`, `-shrink`, `-merge` |\n238\t| `declscope shrink [packages]` | [Unexport what no importer uses](#unexporting-what-no-importer-uses), inside `internal/` | `-fix`, `-config` |\n239\t| `declscope skill install` | Install the authoring and adoption skills for an AI agent | `--agent`, `--scope` |\n240\t\n241\t`declscope <subcommand> -help` lists each one's flags.\n242\t\n243\t## Configuration\n244\t\n245\tEvery setting is optional. The table below lists each setting and its default value. The YAML block shows all available keys; some values are examples.\n246\t\n247\t```yaml\n248\tdefaults:\n249\t  unexported: private     # shared | private\n250\t\n251\trules:\n252\t  naming:\n253\t    qualify: never        # always | never | ondemand\n254\t    exported: false       # true | false\n255\t    vocabulary:\n256\t      mouse: [wheel]\n257\t  boundary: on           # off | on\n258\t  surplus: strict        # off | loose | strict\n259\t  unused: strict         # off | loose | strict\n260\t\n261\tfilter:\n262\t  only: []              # nothing outside these, when set\n263\t  omit:\n264\t    - \"**/mock_*.go\"    # and not these\n265\t\n266\tbaseline: .declscope-baseline.yaml\n267\t```\n268\t\n269\t| Key | Values | Default | Effect |\n270\t| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n271\t| `defaults.unexported` | `shared`, `private` | `private` | Scope of a declaration that carries no directive and inherits none |\n272\t| `rules.naming.qualify` | `always`, `never`, `ondemand` | `never` | When a name must carry its namespace. See [the naming rule](#when-it-applies) |\n273\t| `rules.naming.exported` | `true`, `false` | `false` | Whether the naming rule also reaches exported declarations. The rename is never offered there |\n274\t| `rules.naming.vocabulary` | Namespace to a list of words | None | Extra words that carry a namespace. See [what carries a namespace](#what-carries-a-namespace) |\n275\t| `rules.boundary` | `off`, `on` | `on` | Whether the [`boundary`](#boundary) rule reports. See [reach without a boundary](#reach-without-a-boundary) |\n276\t| `rules.surplus` | `off`, `loose`, `strict` | `strict` | How much the [`surplus`](#surplus) rule reports. See [strict](#strict) |\n277\t| `rules.unused` | `off`, `loose`, `strict` | `strict` | How much the [`unused`](#unused-directives) rule reports. See [off, loose and strict](#off-loose-and-strict) |\n278\t| `filter.only` | Path globs | None | When set, no file outside them is read. Empty places no restriction |\n279\t| `filter.omit` | Path globs | None | Files taken back out, whether or not `only` let them through |\n280\t| `baseline` | A path relative to the config file | The nearest `.declscope-baseline.yaml` | The [baseline](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase) to consult |\n281\t\n282\t> [!TIP]\n283\t> For the recommended checks, put this in `.declscope.yaml`:\n284\t>\n285\t> ```yaml\n286\t> rules:\n287\t>   naming:\n288\t>     qualify: ondemand\n289\t>     exported: true\n290\t> ```\n291\t>\n292\t> `ondemand` checks names once a package has a second namespace. `exported: true` includes exported declarations. `surplus` and `unused` default to `strict`.\n293\t\n294\t- The file is `.declscope.yaml` or `.declscope.yml`. An empty one changes nothing.\n295\t- [`-config`](#flags) names one file, and reads no other.\n296\t- An **unknown key is an error**, and so is a value a key does not accept. The message names what the section does take, so a typo never leaves a rule at its default in silence.\n297\t\n298\t`defaults` takes only `unexported`, because an exported declaration has no scope to default.\n299\t\n300\t### How two config files compose\n301\t\n302\tEvery `.declscope.yaml` between the analyzed package and the module root is read, **outermost first**. A nearer file does not replace the one above it. Each key composes on its own.\n303\t\n304\t| Key | Down the chain |\n305\t| --- | --- |\n306\t| `defaults.*`, `rules.*` except `vocabulary`, `baseline` | The nearest file that states the key wins. A key no file states takes the built-in default |\n307\t| `rules.naming.vocabulary` | Merged per namespace. The nearer file wins the namespaces it states |\n308\t| `filter.only` | **Intersected.** A file is read when it matches every stating file's list |\n309\t| `filter.omit` | **Unioned.** A file matching any level's list is not read |\n310\t\n311\t> [!IMPORTANT]\n312\t> **A config file can only ever shrink what is read.** An `omit` written at the root holds everywhere below it, and no nested file can undo it. `filter` has no negation, so nothing like `.gitignore`'s `!` can put a path back.\n313\t\n314\t### The filter rule\n315\t\n316\t`filter` decides which files are read at all. A file matches a list when it matches **any** pattern in it.\n317\t\n318\t| Written | Read |\n319\t| --- | --- |\n320\t| Neither | Every file |\n321\t| `only` alone | Nothing outside the patterns |\n322\t| `omit` alone | Everything except the patterns |\n323\t| Both | What `only` admits, minus what `omit` names |\n324\t\n325\tAn empty `only` places no restriction, which is why a repository with no config is read whole.\n326\t\n327\tA pattern is read against the directory of **the config file that states it**. Anchoring follows the rules of `.gitignore`.\n328\t\n329\t| Pattern | Matches |\n330\t| --- | --- |\n331\t| `gen.go` | A file of that name at any depth |\n332\t| `/gen.go`, `./gen.go` | The one beside this config file |\n333\t| `gen/**` | That directory beside this config file, and no other |\n334\t| `**/gen/**` | That directory at any depth |\n335\t| `gen/` | That directory at any depth, the same as `**/gen/**` |\n336\t| `/gen/`, `./gen/` | That directory beside this config file, the same as `gen/**` |\n337\t| `*`, `?` | Within one path segment |\n338\t\n339\tA leading `./` anchors the same way as a leading `/`. A trailing `/` names a directory and everything in it. Without one, a pattern names a file, so `./vendor` matches only a file called `vendor`. Write `./vendor/` or `./vendor/**` for the directory.\n340\t\n341\tOne report comes from the configuration rather than from the code. It fires when a file's `only` matches files, but an `only` above it removes them all, so the package is read as empty.\n342\t\n343\t```console\n344\tsub/a.go:1:1: filter.only stated in /repo/sub matches 1 file(s) here, but an only above it removes them all, so this package is read as empty\n345\t```\n346\t\n347\tThe report is that narrow on purpose. A package that reads nothing is usually the point, as with a root `only` naming one subtree, or an `omit` naming a directory.\n348\t\n349\tThe cause is in the config files, so fix it there: change the nested `only`, or the `only` above it, so that the files are read. No directive silences this report, since nothing in the package is read. `filter` is still a valid rule name for `//declscope:ignore`, but such an ignore silences nothing, so the [`unused`](#unused-directives) rule reports it.\n350\t\n351\t## Directives\n352\t\n353\tA **directive** is a line comment `//declscope:name`, with a lowercase name, no spaces, and any argument after a space. Any other comment starting with `declscope:` is [malformed](#malformed-directives). A trailing `// reason` is ignored.\n354\t\n355\t```go\n356\t//declscope:shared // used by the reporting code\n357\t```\n358\t\n359\t| Directive | Level | Effect |\n360\t| --- | --- | --- |\n361\t| `//declscope:shared`, `//declscope:private` | Declaration or file | States the [scope](#scope-resolution). On a type it also reaches the type's [fields](#members), but not its methods |\n362\t| `//declscope:ignore` | Declaration or file | Silences every rule the analyzer reports. [`overexported`](#silencing-it) must be named |\n363\t| `//declscope:ignore <rules>` | Declaration or file | Silences the named [rules](#rules), comma-separated. Naming [`filter`](#the-filter-rule) silences nothing |\n364\t| `//declscope:core` | File | Joins the file to the [core namespace](#the-core-namespace) |\n365\t| `//declscope:namespace <name>` | File | Joins the file to an [explicitly named namespace](#namespaces) |\n366\t\n367\t> [!CAUTION]\n368\t> `//declscope:shared` was spelled `//declscope:package` before v0.19.0, and `defaults.unexported: shared` was `package`. v0.20.0 and later read neither. To upgrade from v0.18.x or earlier, go through v0.19.0 first and run `-fix` there: see [#186](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope/issues/186).\n369\t\n370\t### Placement\n371\t\n372\tA declaration-level directive goes in the doc comment, directly above the declaration. A file-level directive goes above the package clause.\n373\t\n374\t```go\n375\t//declscope:shared\n376\t\n377\tpackage database\n378\t\n379\t//declscope:shared\n380\tfunc userSeed() {}\n381\t```\n382\t\n383\tA directive on a block reaches every spec in it. A directive on one spec overrides the block's.\n384\t\n385\t```go\n386\t//declscope:shared\n387\tvar (\n388\t\tseed  = 1\n389\t\t//declscope:private\n390\t\tlimit = 2 // this one is private\n391\t)\n392\t```\n393\t\n394\tA directive on a type reaches its fields and its interface method names. It does not reach its methods, which take their own file's level.\n395\t\n396\t<details>\n397\t<summary>Where a file-level directive may sit</summary>\n398\t\n399\t`//declscope:namespace` must come before the package clause. Three placements are accepted there.\n400\t\n401\t<table>\n402\t<thead>\n403\t<tr><th>Placement</th><th>Example</th></tr>\n404\t</thead>\n405\t<tbody>\n406\t<tr>\n407\t<td>A blank line before <code>package</code>, as this README writes</td>\n408\t<td>\n409\t\n410\t```go\n411\t//declscope:namespace billing\n412\t\n413\tpackage app\n414\t```\n415\t\n416\t</td>\n417\t</tr>\n418\t<tr>\n419\t<td>Directly above <code>package</code></td>\n420\t<td>\n421\t\n422\t```go\n423\t//declscope:namespace billing\n424\tpackage app\n425\t```\n426\t\n427\t</td>\n428\t</tr>\n429\t<tr>\n430\t<td>At the bottom of the package doc comment, after a blank <code>//</code> line: Go's own convention for a directive in a doc comment</td>\n431\t<td>\n432\t\n433\t```go\n434\t// Package app bills users.\n435\t//\n436\t//declscope:namespace billing\n437\tpackage app\n438\t```\n439\t\n440\t</td>\n441\t</tr>\n442\t</tbody>\n443\t</table>\n444\t\n445\tGo excludes a `//tool:name` comment from a doc comment, so none of them reaches the rendered documentation.\n446\t\n447\t</details>\n448\t\n449\t### Ignore levels\n450\t\n451\t- Every level is consulted. An ignore counts as used whenever it covers a rule that would have fired, so overlapping ignores never make one another look unused.\n452\t- Ignores are consulted **before** the baseline. A suppression the baseline would also have absorbed still counts as used.\n453\t\n454\t### Unused directives\n455\t\n456\tThe `unused` rule reports a directive that changes nothing. A directive that declscope cannot read belongs to the [`directive`](#malformed-directives) rule instead.\n457\t\n458\t#### Off, loose and strict\n459\t\n460\t| `rules.unused` | `//declscope:ignore` is reported when | `//declscope:shared` or `//declscope:private` is reported when | `-fix` |\n461\t| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n462\t| `off` | Never | Never | None |\n463\t| `loose` | It silenced no report | Deleting it would change no declaration's scope under any config | None |\n464\t| `strict` *(default)* | It silenced no report | Deleting it would change no declaration's scope under the current config | Deletes a redundant scope directive, unless [withheld](#the-strict-fix) |\n465\t\n466\t- One comment gets one report, however many declarations it reaches. A block's directive is reported once.\n467\t- Without the directive, a declaration falls to the next row of [scope resolution](#scope-resolution). Only `defaults.unexported` there depends on the config.\n468\t- Under `strict`, a directive that `loose` keeps also stays when deleting it would make a nearer directive redundant.\n469\t- `off` still leaves the `directive` rule on.\n470\t- An ignore of `boundary` is not reported where a file the build leaves out names a declaration it reaches, or for a field, its type: a literal written by position names only the type. That file may cross into it under another build tag, where the ignore silences the crossing. The run that reads the file still reports an ignore with nothing to silence.\n471\t\n472\t> [!WARNING]\n473\t> Under `strict`, changing `defaults.unexported` changes the reports. With `unexported: shared`, every `//declscope:shared` on an unexported declaration that nothing else widens is reported, and one `-fix` run deletes them. `loose` never reports a directive only because it names the current default.\n474\t\n475\t<details>\n476\t<summary>Example: one file under each mode</summary>\n477\t\n478\t```go\n479\tpackage app\n480\t\n481\ttype user struct {\n482\t\t//declscope:private\n483\t\tname string\n484\t}\n485\t\n486\t//declscope:shared\n487\tfunc Helper() {}\n488\t\n489\t//declscope:ignore boundary\n490\tfunc greet(u user) string { return u.name }\n491\t```\n492\t\n493\t| Line | `off` | `loose` | `strict` |\n494\t| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n495\t| 4 | Nothing | Nothing | `unused //declscope:private on user.name: it already has private scope` |\n496\t| 8 | Nothing | `unused //declscope:shared on Helper: nothing it reaches takes a scope` | `unused //declscope:shared on Helper: it already has shared scope` |\n497\t| 11 | Nothing | `unused //declscope:ignore boundary on greet` | `unused //declscope:ignore boundary on greet` |\n498\t\n499\tLine 4 is where the modes differ. Deleting line 4 leaves `user.name` private only because `defaults.unexported` is private, which `loose` does not rely on.\n500\t\n501\t</details>\n502\t\n503\t#### Report messages\n504\t\n505\tEvery unused report names the directive and says why it is unused. `loose` and `strict` word the reason differently.\n506\t\n507\t#### The strict fix\n508\t\n509\t`-fix` deletes a directive that `strict` reports, unless deleting it would change another report. Then the report stays, with no fix.\n510\t\n511\t<details>\n512\t<summary>Example: one directive deleted, one withheld</summary>\n513\t\n514\t```go\n515\t// user.go\n516\tpackage app\n517\t\n518\t//declscope:private\n519\tfunc normalize() {}\n520\t\n521\t//declscope:private\n522\tfunc trim() {}\n523\t```\n524\t\n525\t```go\n526\t// order.go\n527\tpackage app\n528\t\n529\tvar _ = normalize\n530\t```\n531\t\n532\t```console\n533\t$ declscope ./...    # with rules.unused: strict\n534\tuser.go:4:6: func normalize is declared private by //declscope:private, but is used from namespace \"order\"\n535\torder.go:3:9: \tused here, in namespace \"order\"\n536\tuser.go:3:1: unused //declscope:private on normalize: it already has private scope\n537\tuser.go:6:1: unused //declscope:private on trim: it already has private scope\n538\t```\n539\t\n540\t`-fix` changes `user.go`. The `boundary` report names `normalize`'s directive, so that one stays.\n541\t\n542\t```diff\n543\t //declscope:private\n544\t func normalize() {}\n545\t \n546\t-//declscope:private\n547\t func trim() {}\n548\t```\n549\t\n550\t</details>\n551\t\n552\t#### Silencing an unused report\n553\t\n554\t| Ignore | Silences the unused report of |\n555\t| --- | --- |\n556\t| `//declscope:ignore unused` on a declaration | Every other directive on that declaration |\n557\t| Bare `//declscope:ignore` on a declaration | The scope directive on that declaration. Not the other ignores there, so a group of ignores cannot excuse one another |\n558\t| `//declscope:ignore unused`, or a bare one, above the package clause | Every other directive in the file |\n559\t| Any ignore on a type or a block | Nothing inside it. For other rules it reaches inside, but here one ignore would hide every stale directive under it |\n560\t\n561\t**No ignore silences its own unused report.**\n562\t\n563\t<details>\n564\t<summary>Example</summary>\n565\t\n566\t```go\n567\tpackage app\n568\t\n569\t//declscope:shared\n570\t//declscope:ignore unused\n571\tfunc A() {}\n572\t\n573\t//declscope:shared\n574\t//declscope:ignore directive\n575\tfunc B() {}\n576\t\n577\t//declscope:ignore unused\n578\ttype T struct {\n579\t\t//declscope:shared\n580\t\tF int\n581\t}\n582\t\n583\t//declscope:ignore qualify\n584\t//declscope:ignore unused\n585\tfunc C() {}\n586\t\n587\t//declscope:ignore unused\n588\tfunc D() {}\n589\t```\n590\t\n591\t```console\n592\t$ declscope ./...\n593\tuser.go:7:1: unused //declscope:shared on B: it already has shared scope\n594\tuser.go:13:2: unused //declscope:shared on T.F: it already has shared scope\n595\tuser.go:8:1: unused //declscope:ignore directive on B\n596\tuser.go:11:1: unused //declscope:ignore unused on T\n597\tuser.go:21:1: unused //declscope:ignore unused on D\n598\t```\n599\t\n600\t| Declaration | Result | Why |\n601\t| --- | --- | --- |\n602\t| `A` | Quiet | `ignore unused` silences the scope directive's report |\n603\t| `B` | Both reported | `ignore directive` names another rule, so it silenced nothing |\n604\t| `T` | Both reported | The type's ignore does not reach the field |\n605\t| `C` | Quiet | `ignore unused` silences the report on `ignore qualify` |\n606\t| `D` | Reported | Its only candidate is its own report |\n607\t\n608\t</details>\n609\t\n610\t### Malformed directives\n611\t\n612\tOnly `//declscope:name` is a directive. Any other comment starting with `declscope:`, and an unknown, conflicting or misplaced directive, is reported by the `directive` rule and has no effect.\n613\t\n614\t<details>\n615\t<summary>Every malformed-directive report</summary>\n616\t\n617\tThe rule is always on, and has no configuration key. `//declscope:ignore directive` silences it, on the declaration or above the package clause.\n618\t\n619\t`<name>` stands for the directive's own name, such as `shared` or `core`.\n620\t\n621\t| Directive | Report |\n622\t| --- | --- |\n623\t| `//declscope:foo` on a declaration | `unknown directive declscope:foo` |\n624\t| `//declscope:foo` above the package clause | `declscope:foo is not a file-level directive` |\n625\t| `// declscope:shared`, `/*declscope:shared*/`, or any other comment starting with `declscope:` that is not `//declscope:name` | `malformed declscope directive: write it as //declscope:name` |\n626\t| `//declscope:shared x`, or an argument to another directive that takes none | `//declscope:<name> takes no argument` |\n627\t| `//declscope:namespace` with no name | `declscope:namespace requires a name` |\n628\t| `//declscope:namespace Billing` | `namespace \"Billing\" is not a valid lowerCamelCase identifier` |\n629\t| `//declscope:private` and `//declscope:shared` together | `conflicting scope directives: ...` |\n630\t| `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:namespace` together | `conflicting namespace directives: a core file's namespace is the core` |\n631\t| `//declscope:ignore foo` | `unknown rule \"foo\" in declscope:ignore (want one of boundary, qualify, surplus, unused, directive, filter, overexported)` |\n632\t| `//declscope:ignore ,` or `//declscope:ignore boundary,` | `empty rule name in declscope:ignore` |\n633\t| The same directive twice on one declaration or file. Two ignores naming the same rules, in any order, count as the same directive | `duplicate declscope:<name> directive`, at the second |\n634\t| `//declscope:namespace` or `//declscope:core` after the package clause | `declscope:<name> must appear before the package clause` |\n635\t| A valid `shared`, `private` or `ignore` directive attached to no declaration, such as one inside a function body | `misplaced declscope:<name>: no declaration here for it to bind to; ...` |\n636\t\n637\t</details>\n638\t\n639\t## Namespaces\n640\t\n641\tA **namespace** is the unit within which a `private` declaration may be used. By default each file is its own namespace, named after the file.\n642\t\n643\t| File | Namespace |\n644\t| --- | --- |\n645\t| `user_repository.go` | `userRepository` |\n646\t| `user_repository_test.go` | `userRepository`. A test shares the namespace of its subject |\n647\t| `parser_linux.go` | `parser`. A GOOS or GOARCH suffix is a build constraint, not a namespace |\n648\t| `parser_test_linux.go` | `parserTest`. As in go/build, only a name ending in `_test.go` is a test |\n649\t| `parser_linux.pb.go`, `parser.x_linux.go` | `parserPb`, `parserXLinux`. As in go/build, a suffix counts only before the first dot |\n650\t| `user_id.go`, `user_ids.go`, `parse_json.go` | `userID`, `userIDs`, `parseJSON`. An initialism, or its plural, is spelled the way Go spells it |\n651\t| `foo-bar.go`, `Foo.go` | `fooBar`, `foo`. Any separator, and a PascalCase stem, become lowerCamelCase |\n652\t| `HTTPServer.go`, `URLs.go`, `IPv4.go` | `httpServer`, `urls`, `ipv4`. A leading initialism is lowered the way Go lowers one |\n653\t| `2fa_auth.go`, `用户.go` | `2faAuth`, `用户`. Valid namespaces, but never a prefix: the first character must be a letter with a capital form |\n654\t\n655\tThe namespace comes *from* the file name and is not equal to it. So you can rename a file without renaming what it declares.\n656\t\n657\tFiles join an **explicitly named** namespace with a directive before the package clause. This is how one unit spans several files. The name must be an unexported identifier.\n658\t\n659\t```go\n660\t//declscope:namespace user\n661\tpackage repo\n662\t```\n663\t\n664\t### The core namespace\n665\t\n666\tOne namespace in a package may be its **core**: the unit the package is named for. Several files may carry `//declscope:core`, and they share the one core namespace.\n667\t\n668\t```go\n669\t// client.go\n670\t//declscope:core\n671\t\n672\tpackage transport\n673\t```\n674\t\n675\tThe core has no prefix, so [the naming rule](#the-naming-rule) asks nothing of its declarations. No prefix still names exactly one unit.\n676\t\n677\tA test file joins the core when it tests a core file, as `client_test.go` tests `client.go`. The test file is matched by its whole name, so `client_linux_test.go` joins a core `client_linux.go` but not a core `client.go`. Only a test file joins: a core `client_test.go` does not take `client.go` into the core, and a core `client_linux.go` does not take `client.go`. A test file that names its own namespace with `//declscope:namespace` keeps it.\n678\t\n679\t> [!IMPORTANT]\n680\t> `//declscope:core` sets the namespace and nothing else. It carries no scope. A core declaration still takes [`defaults.unexported`](#configuration): by default it is private *to the core*, and a file outside the core that names it crosses a boundary.\n681\t>\n682\t> | Written on a file | Effect |\n683\t> | --- | --- |\n684\t> | `//declscope:core` | The file joins the core. What it declares keeps the default scope |\n685\t> | `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:shared` | Both apply. The file is core, and what it declares is package-wide |\n686\t> | `//declscope:core` and `//declscope:namespace` | Refused. A core file's namespace *is* the core |\n687\t\n688\t## Scopes\n689\t\n690\tThe **subject** of the analysis is a package's unexported surface: its unexported package-level declarations, and the unexported [members](#members) of any type.\n691\t\n692\tA **scope** is how far a declaration may be used. There are two.\n693\t\n694\t| Scope | Meaning | Rust equivalent |\n695\t| --- | --- | --- |\n696\t| `shared` | Usable anywhere in the package | `pub(super)` |\n697\t| `private` | Usable only inside its own [namespace](#namespaces) | No modifier |\n698\t\n699\tThere is no `public`. Go already spells that with a capital letter, and declscope never sees a use beyond the package edge.\n700\t\n701\t### Scope resolution\n702\t\n703\tA declaration's scope comes from the first row that applies.\n704\t\n705\t| The declaration | Scope |\n706\t| --- | --- |\n707\t| Carries `//declscope:shared` or `//declscope:private` | The directive's |\n708\t| Is contained by something that carries one | The container's |\n709\t| Sits in a file carrying a [file-level directive](#directives) | The file's |\n710\t| Is exported | `shared` |\n711\t| Otherwise | [`defaults.unexported`](#configuration), which is `private` unless configured |\n712\t\n713\tContainment means a [field](#members) inside its type, or a spec inside its `var`, `const` or `type` block.\n714\t\n715\tAn unexported declaration is `shared` only where something says so: a directive, or the `defaults` key. Its *name* plays no part. A prefix marks ownership and grants nothing.\n716\t\n717\t> [!IMPORTANT]\n718\t> Exportedness decides the default, and nothing else. An **exported field of an unexported type** still resolves to `shared`, so making the type unexported protects nothing.\n719\t>\n720\t> State the boundary instead. `//declscope:private` on the type binds every field it reaches.\n721\t>\n722\t> ```go\n723\t> // Capitalized for encoding/json, not for an audience.\n724\t> //declscope:private\n725\t> type entry struct {\n726\t> \tKey   string `json:\"key\"`\n727\t> \tValue []byte `json:\"value\"`\n728\t> }\n729\t> ```\n730\t\n731\t### Members\n732\t\n733\tA **member** is a name written *inside* a type's declaration: a struct's **field**, or an interface's **method name**. It is written inside its type, so its namespace is the type's file's, and the type's directive reaches it.\n734\t\n735\tA **method with a receiver** is not a member. It is an ordinary top-level declaration, and its own file gives it its namespace.\n736\t\n737\t| | Package-level declaration | Member | Method with a receiver |\n738\t| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n739\t| Bounding namespace | Its file's | Its **type**'s file's | Its file's |\n740\t| Contained by | Its `var`, `const` or `type` block | Its **type** | Nothing |\n741\t| [Naming rule](#the-naming-rule) | Applies | Does not apply | Only when filed away from its type |\n742\t\n743\tThe naming rule skips members because a member is never read on its own. Every use writes its value first, so `u.name` hands the reader `u` to follow. A method is read the same way, through its receiver.\n744\t\n745\tWhat Go lacks for a member is encapsulation. Every unexported field is visible to the whole package. The `private` scope supplies it.\n746\t\n747\t<details>\n748\t<summary>A type's methods filed in another file</summary>\n749\t\n750\tSplitting a type's methods across files is ordinary Go. A builder often declares its state in one file and its chainable methods in another.\n751\t\n752\t```go\n753\t// statement.go   (namespace: statement)\n754\tpackage database\n755\t\n756\ttype Statement struct {\n757\t\tTable  string\n758\t\twheres []string\n759\t}\n760\t```\n761\t```go\n762\t// query.go   (namespace: query)\n763\tpackage database\n764\t\n765\tfunc (s *Statement) Where(cond string) *Statement {\n766\t\ts.wheres = append(s.wheres, cond)\n767\t\treturn s\n768\t}\n769\t```\n770\t\n771\tWriting `Where` in `query.go` is not itself a crossing. The field it reaches is one, and the report lands on `statement.go`.\n772\t\n773\t```console\n774\t$ declscope ./...\n775\tstatement.go:5:2: field Statement.wheres is private to namespace \"statement\", but is used from namespace \"query\"\n776\tquery.go:4:4: \tused here, in namespace \"query\"\n777\tquery.go:4:22: \tused here, in namespace \"query\"\n778\t```\n779\t\n780\tThe naming rule asks the method to carry `query`. A method is read through its receiver, and `s.Where` points the reader at `Statement`'s unit, which does not hold it.\n781\t\n782\t```console\n783\tquery.go:3:21: method Where does not carry namespace \"query\" anywhere in its name; rename it to QueryWhere, or to another name that carries \"query\"\n784\t```\n785\t\n786\tNeither report asks for a rename here. The two files are one unit split in two, and `//declscope:namespace statement` on `query.go` settles both.\n787\t\n788\t</details>\n789\t\n790\t> [!TIP]\n791\t> An unexported interface method is the **sealed interface** idiom. Only this package can spell the name, so only this package can implement the interface. declscope gives it file granularity.\n792\t>\n793\t> Satisfying an interface is **not** a use of the name, because a method set is resolved, not written. Naming the method does cross.\n794\t\n795\t> [!WARNING]\n796\t> Operations on the **whole value** name no field: copying it, comparing it, zeroing it. They are outside what declscope can see. See [Limits](#limits).\n797\t\n798\t## Rules\n799\t\n800\tA **rule** is one check. A rule's name is the diagnostic's category, its [baseline](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase) key, and what [`//declscope:ignore`](#directives) targets.\n801\t\n802\t| Rule | Reports | Fix | Configured by | Default |\n803\t| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n804\t| [`boundary`](#boundary) | A declaration used from outside the namespace it is private to | Insert `//declscope:shared` | `rules.boundary` | `on` |\n805\t| [`qualify`](#the-naming-rule) | A name that does not carry its namespace | Rename to prefix it | `rules.naming.*` | Off |\n806\t| [`surplus`](#surplus) | Shared scope with no visible use from another namespace | Under `strict`, insert `//declscope:private` | `rules.surplus` | `strict` |\n807\t| [`unused`](#unused-directives) | An ignore that silenced nothing, or a scope directive that changes no scope | Under `strict`, delete a redundant scope directive | `rules.unused` | `strict` |\n808\t| [`directive`](#malformed-directives) | A directive that is malformed, unknown, conflicting or misplaced | None | No | On |\n809\t| [`filter`](#the-filter-rule) | A `filter.only` that an `only` above it cancels | None | No | On |\n810\t| [`overexported`](#unexporting-what-no-importer-uses) | An exported declaration of an `internal/` package that nothing outside its package uses | Unexport it | Running `declscope shrink` | Not run by the analyzer |\n811\t\n812\tEvery diagnostic carries **at most one** fix, so `-fix` never has to choose.\n813\t\n814\t### `boundary`\n815\t\n816\t`boundary` reports a `private` declaration used from outside its namespace. For a [member](#members), the boundary is the namespace of its type. The [example above](#what-it-reports) is this rule.\n817\t\n818\tThe message names where the scope came from.\n819\t\n820\t| Where the scope came from | Message |\n821\t| --- | --- |\n822\t| `defaults` | `func normalizeEmail is private to namespace \"userRepository\", but is used from namespace \"orderRepository\"` |\n823\t| The declaration's own directive | `func normalizeEmail is declared private by //declscope:private, but is used from namespace \"orderRepository\"` |\n824\t| Its type's directive | `field Statement.wheres is declared private by //declscope:private on Statement, but is used from namespace \"query\"` |\n825\t| A file-level directive | `func normalizeEmail is declared private by the file's //declscope:private, but is used from namespace \"orderRepository\"` |\n826\t\n827\tEvery crossing use site is attached to the diagnostic, and a use from inside the declaration's own namespace is not. The report lands on the **declaration**, not on the use.\n828\t\n829\t| Case | Fix |\n830\t| --- | --- |\n831\t| The declaration states its **own** scope | None. The directive and the use are both deliberate, and `-fix` must not overwrite what the author wrote |\n832\t| The `private` is inherited from a type or a file | Offered. The inserted directive sits on the declaration, which outranks both |\n833\t| A type and its members cross together | One directive, on the type. The members are reported without a fix, since a second directive on them would bind nothing |\n834\t\n835\t#### Reach without a boundary\n836\t\n837\t`rules.boundary: off` switches this rule off. What is left is the naming rule, for a repository that wants the ownership mark in a name without the scope behind it.\n838\t\n839\t```yaml\n840\trules:\n841\t  naming:\n842\t    qualify: ondemand\n843\t  boundary: off\n844\t  surplus: off\n845\t```\n846\t\n847\tSet `surplus: off` alongside it. `surplus` audits `//declscope:shared`, which means nothing once reach is not checked.\n848\t\n849\t> [!TIP]\n850\t> This is not how to adopt declscope gradually. A [baseline](#adopting-on-an-existing-codebase) records what a codebase already has and still reports what is new. A switch reports nothing, so you never learn what turning it on later would cost.\n851\t\n852\t### The naming rule\n853\t\n854\t**Off by default.** Turn it on with `rules.naming.qualify`.\n855\t\n856\tThe rule asks a package-level declaration to carry its file's namespace somewhere in its name. The name then says which unit owns it, at the call site and in a stack trace.\n857\t\n858\t```go\n859\t// order_repository.go\n860\tfunc scanOrder(rows *sql.Rows) (domain.Order, error) {\n861\t\t// ...\n862\t\to.BuyerEmail = normalizeEmail(email) // the email unit's, and shared\n863\t}\n864\t```\n865\t\n866\tThe mark grants nothing. Reach is stated by [scope](#scope-resolution) alone.\n867\t\n868\t> [!NOTE]\n869\t> The rule is opt-in because whether a prefix reads well depends on the file name, and no tool can see that. A prefix from `comments.go` reads as a noun phrase, `commentsAttached`. A prefix from `collect.go` reads as a command, `collectAddFunc`.\n870\t\n871\t#### When it applies\n872\t\n873\t| `rules.naming.qualify` | Effect |\n874\t| --- | --- |\n875\t| `never` *(default)* | Off |\n876\t| `ondemand` | Required once the package has a **second namespace**. A file holding only a package clause and comments, as a `doc.go` usually does, is not counted |\n877\t| `always` | Required in every package, so that gaining a second namespace is not a mass rename |\n878\t\n879\t<details>\n880\t<summary>Declarations the rule never reaches</summary>\n881\t\n882\t[Members](#members) and [the core namespace](#the-core-namespace) are explained in their own sections.\n883\t\n884\t<table>\n885\t<thead>\n886\t<tr><th>Declaration</th><th>Example</th><th>Reason</th></tr>\n887\t</thead>\n888\t<tbody>\n889\t<tr>\n890\t<td>A member, or a method written beside its type</td>\n891\t<td>\n892\t\n893\t```go\n894\t// user.go\n895\ttype user struct{ name string }\n896\t\n897\tfunc (u user) greet() string { return u.name }\n898\t```\n899\t\n900\t</td>\n901\t<td>Already qualified by that type at every use</td>\n902\t</tr>\n903\t<tr>\n904\t<td><code>func main</code> in package <code>main</code></td>\n905\t<td>\n906\t\n907\t```go\n908\t// cmd/app/run.go\n909\tpackage main\n910\t\n911\tfunc main() {}\n912\t```\n913\t\n914\t</td>\n915\t<td>A name the toolchain requires</td>\n916\t</tr>\n917\t<tr>\n918\t<td>A test function in a <code>_test.go</code> file</td>\n919\t<td>\n920\t\n921\t```go\n922\t// user_test.go\n923\tfunc TestGreet(t *testing.T) {}\n924\tfunc BenchmarkGreet(b *testing.B) {}\n925\tfunc ExampleGreet() {}\n926\t```\n927\t\n928\t</td>\n929\t<td>The same. <code>go test</code> finds <code>TestXxx</code>, <code>BenchmarkXxx</code>, <code>FuzzXxx</code> and <code>ExampleXxx</code> by name</td>\n930\t</tr>\n931\t<tr>\n932\t<td>A declaration in a namespace that cannot start an identifier</td>\n933\t<td>\n934\t\n935\t```go\n936\t// 2fa.go\n937\tfunc verify() bool { return true }\n938\t```\n939\t\n940\t</td>\n941\t<td>The fix prefixes, and no identifier begins with a digit. A namespace whose first letter has no capital form, such as <code>用户</code> or <code>_foo</code>, is skipped too: an exported name could not take it and stay exported</td>\n942\t</tr>\n943\t<tr>\n944\t<td>An exported identifier, unless <code>rules.naming.exported</code> is on</td>\n945\t<td>\n946\t\n947\t```go\n948\t// user.go\n949\tfunc Greet() {}\n950\t```\n951\t\n952\t</td>\n953\t<td>How the API is spelled is the author's decision</td>\n954\t</tr>\n955\t<tr>\n956\t<td>A declaration in the core namespace</td>\n957\t<td>\n958\t\n959\t```go\n960\t//declscope:core\n961\t\n962\tpackage app\n963\t\n964\tfunc open() {}\n965\t```\n966\t\n967\t</td>\n968\t<td>The core has no prefix</td>\n969\t</tr>\n970\t</tbody>\n971\t</table>\n972\t\n973\t</details>\n974\t\n975\t#### What carries a namespace\n976\t\n977\tThe namespace must appear in the name, ignoring case, starting at a **word boundary**. The match may end inside a word.\n978\t\n979\t| In `user_id.go`, namespace `userID` | Carries it |\n980\t| --- | --- |\n981\t| `userIDCache`, `userIdCache` | Yes |\n982\t| `loadUserID`, `parseUserIds` | Yes. Anywhere in the name, and the right edge may run on |\n983\t| `poweruserID` | No. `user` does not start a word there |\n984\t| `user` in `user.go` | Yes. The name is the namespace |\n985\t\n986\tThe left edge is anchored because the right one is not. Without the anchor, `key` would be found in `monkey`.\n987\t\n988\tTwo English inflections change the namespace's own spelling. Both are accepted.\n989\t\n990\t| Namespace | Also carried by |\n991\t| --- | --- |\n992\t| `store` | `storing`. The final `e` drops before `ing` |\n993\t| `apply` | `applies`, `applied`. The final `y` turns to `i` |\n994\t\n995\tOnly these whole forms are generated, from the namespace's side. The name is never stemmed, so `story` and `storm` do not carry `store`.\n996\t\n997\t**The reverse is not generated**: in `tracing.go`, `traceValue` is reported. The message names the vocabulary key to add.\n998\t\n999\t`rules.naming.vocabulary` lists extra words that carry a namespace. A listed word goes through the same test, so `wheelDelta` carries `mouse` and `pinwheel` does not.\n1000\t\n1001\t```yaml\n1002\trules:\n1003\t  naming:\n1004\t    vocabulary:\n1005\t      mouse: [wheel]\n1006\t      index: [indices]\n1007\t      tracing: [trace]\n1008\t```\n1009\t\n1010\t> [!WARNING]\n1011\t> The vocabulary is for the irregular few. A namespace that needs a long list is a sign that the file declares things it is not about. Splitting the file says more than listing them.\n1012\t\n1013\t#### The rename\n1014\t\n1015\tThe fix prefixes, keeping Go's spelling of an initialism and the original exportedness.\n1016\t\n1017\t| Case | Example | Never |\n1018\t| --- | --- | --- |\n1019\t| Unexported | `id` → `userID` | `userId` |\n1020\t| Exported, under `rules.naming.exported` | `Load` → `UserLoad` | `userLoad` |\n1021\t\n1022\tThe suggestion is one answer, not the only one. Any spelling that carries the namespace settles the rule. A rename never changes what a name is visible to.\n1023\t\n1024\t> [!NOTE]\n1025\t> Sometimes the namespace is what is wrong, not the name. A file name may hold words that name no unit.\n1026\t>\n1027\t> ```console\n1028\t> user_repository.go:18:6: func scanUser does not carry namespace \"userRepository\" anywhere in its name; rename it to userRepositoryScanUser, or to another name that carries \"userRepository\"\n1029\t> ```\n1030\t>\n1031\t> The unit here is `user`, not `userRepository`. `//declscope:namespace user` on the file settles the rule and leaves every name alone.\n1032\t\n1033\t#### Withheld renames\n1034\t\n1035\tA rename is offered only when it provably changes nothing but the spelling. The violation is reported either way. A doubt withholds the fix, never the diagnostic.\n1036\t\n1037\t> [!CAUTION]\n1038\t> Go resolves a name from the inside out, so a new name that is free at package level can still be bound at a use site. The wrong rename **compiles and computes something else**.\n1039\t>\n1040\t> ```go\n1041\t> var count = 10\n1042\t> func Add(fooCount int) int { return fooCount + count } // Add(1) == 11\n1043\t> ```\n1044\t> ```go\n1045\t> // after a careless rename of count to fooCount\n1046\t> func Add(fooCount int) int { return fooCount + fooCount } // Add(1) == 2\n1047\t> ```\n1048\t\n1049\tA method, or a type that is embedded, is renamed only when the new name is free on every type that holds it. A method is also not renamed when an interface of the package asks for its old or new name, since a type assertion would change its answer.\n1050\t\n1051\tA package that holds a non-Go source file, such as assembly (`.s`) for any architecture, gets no rename fix. Assembly names Go functions by text, which the rename cannot follow, and the build would fail at link time. Rename by hand, or add `//declscope:ignore qualify`.\n1052\t\n1053\t### `surplus`\n1054\t\n1055\t`surplus` is the converse of `boundary`. It reports shared scope that no visible use from another namespace needs.\n1056\t\n1057\t| `rules.surplus` | Reports | Fix |\n1058\t| --- | --- | --- |\n1059\t| `off` | Nothing | |\n1060\t| `loose` | A `//declscope:shared` that nothing it reaches needs | None |\n1061\t| `strict` *(default)* | What `loose` reports, plus each declaration a directive in use widens for nothing | Insert `//declscope:private` |\n1062\t\n1063\t```go\n1064\t// email.go\n1065\tpackage database\n1066\t\n1067\t//declscope:shared\n1068\tfunc normalizeEmail(s string) string { return s }\n1069\t```\n1070\t\n1071\t```console\n1072\t$ declscope ./...\n1073\temail.go:3:1: //declscope:shared on normalizeEmail: no use from another namespace is visible to declscope\n1074\t```\n1075\t\n1076\tOne comment gets one report, however many declarations take their scope from it. A declaration that states its own scope does not depend on the comment, so it neither keeps it alive nor appears under it.\n1077\t\n1078\t> [!IMPORTANT]\n1079\t> The rule concludes from an **absence**. A directive can hold up something declscope cannot see, so the rule stays quiet on any doubt. For the same reason `loose` offers no fix: its advice is to delete a directive.\n1080\t\n1081\t#### `strict`\n1082\t\n1083\tUnder `loose`, one used declaration keeps its whole directive quiet. The rest of what the directive reaches may still be wider than it needs. `strict` reports each of those, and `-fix` narrows it.\n1084\t\n1085\t```go\n1086\t// account.go\n1087\tpackage bank\n1088\t\n1089\t//declscope:shared\n1090\ttype account struct {\n1091\t\tid      int\n1092\t\tbalance int\n1093\t}\n1094\t\n1095\tfunc accountDeposit(a *account, n int) { a.balance += n }\n1096\t```\n1097\t\n1098\t```go\n1099\t// ledger.go\n1100\tpackage bank\n1101\t\n1102\tfunc ledgerKey(a account) int { return a.id }\n1103\t```\n1104\t\n1105\t```console\n1106\t$ declscope ./...\n1107\taccount.go:6:2: field account.balance takes shared scope from //declscope:shared on account, but no use from another namespace is visible to declscope\n1108\t```\n1109\t\n1110\t`-fix` changes `account.go`:\n1111\t\n1112\t```diff\n1113\t //declscope:shared\n1114\t type account struct {\n1115\t-\tid      int\n1116\t+\tid int\n1117\t+\t//declscope:private\n1118\t \tbalance int\n1119\t }\n1120\t```\n1121\t\n1122\tEvery enclosing directive is judged the same way.\n1123\t\n1124\t| The directive is on | Judged one by one |\n1125\t| --- | --- |\n1126\t| A struct or interface type | Each field, or each method name |\n1127\t| A `var`, `const` or `type` block | Each spec |\n1128\t| The file | Each declaration in the file, and each member of a type that states no scope |\n1129\t\n1130\t`strict` is the default. `loose` checks only directives as a whole; select it explicitly if that is the policy your repository wants.\n1131\t\n1132\t> [!TIP]\n1133\t> Convention puts private fields last, after the fields other namespaces read. The fix never reorders fields: order is observable through unkeyed composite literals, positional encodings, `unsafe` offsets and 64-bit atomic alignment. Move them yourself where none of those apply.\n1134\t\n1135\t## Unexporting what no importer uses\n1136\t\n1137\t`declscope shrink` finds the exported declarations of `internal/` packages that nothing outside their package uses. With `-fix` it unexports them.\n1138\t\n1139\t**Why it matters.** An exported declaration takes shared scope by default, so the analyzer never reports a boundary on it. An exported name that nothing outside needs hides a declaration from every check here. Unexported, it takes `private`, and the analyzer checks who reaches it.\n1140\t\n1141\t**Why a subcommand.** The analyzer reads one package, and any importer might use an exported name. Inside `internal/`, Go limits the importers to one directory tree. `shrink` loads the whole module, so it sees every one of them. In a workspace, it loads every module of the workspace. A nested module whose path lies under an `internal/` parent can import the package too, so `shrink` loads it as well, and counts its uses. `go vet` and golangci-lint never run it.\n1142\t\n1143\t```go\n1144\t// internal/user/user.go\n1145\tpackage user\n1146\t\n1147\timport \"fmt\"\n1148\t\n1149\tfunc Load(id int) string { return Format(id) }\n1150\t\n1151\t// Format renders an ID for display.\n1152\tfunc Format(id int) string { return fmt.Sprint(id) }\n1153\t\n1154\ttype Record struct {\n1155\t\tID   int\n1156\t\tName string\n1157\t}\n1158\t\n1159\tfunc Dump(r Record) { fmt.Println(r) }\n1160\t```\n1161\t\n1162\t`api/api.go` calls `user.Load` and names `user.Dump`. Nothing outside `user` names `Format` or `Record`:\n1163\t\n1164\t```console\n1165\t$ declscope shrink\n1166\tinternal/user/user.go:8:6: func Format is exported, but nothing outside example.com/app/internal/user uses it\n1167\t```\n1168\t\n1169\t`declscope shrink -fix` renames `Format` to `format`, and the doc comment that opens with it. `Record` is not reported: `fmt.Println` reads its fields through reflection, which is a use.\n1170\t\n1171\t### Run it before the analyzer\n1172\t\n1173\t**Apply `shrink -fix` first, then work on the analyzer's reports.** A declaration it unexports becomes private to its namespace. Wherever another file uses it, the analyzer now reports a crossing, which `declscope -fix` or a move settles. The other order takes a second round.\n1174\t\n1175\t```console\n1176\t$ declscope shrink -fix ./...\n1177\t$ declscope ./...\n1178\t```\n1179\t\n1180\tRun them in the same order in CI. `shrink` exits 3 when it reports anything, as the analyzer does. With `-fix`, only the reports left without a fix count.\n1181\t\n1182\t### Patterns\n1183\t\n1184\tThe patterns only choose which packages are reported. To find uses, `shrink` always reads every package of the module, whatever the patterns name.\n1185\t\n1186\tFor example, this reports only on `internal/user`:\n1187\t\n1188\t```console\n1189\t$ declscope shrink ./internal/user/...\n1190\tinternal/user/user.go:8:6: func Format is exported, but nothing outside example.com/app/internal/user uses it\n1191\t```\n1192\t\n1193\t`Load` is not reported, although `api/` is outside the pattern. `api/api.go` calls `user.Load`, and that call is a use.\n1194\t\n1195\tOtherwise, a pattern behaves as it does for `go vet`.\n1196\t\n1197\t<details>\n1198\t<summary>What counts as a use, and when the fix is withheld</summary>\n1199\t\n1200\tA fix is offered only where no use can exist outside the package. Where a use may exist but cannot be proved, the report stays and says why no fix is offered.\n1201\t\n1202\t<table>\n1203\t<thead>\n1204\t<tr><th>Code</th><th>Result</th></tr>\n1205\t</thead>\n1206\t<tbody>\n1207\t<tr>\n1208\t<td>\n1209\t\n1210\t```go\n1211\t// internal/user/user.go\n1212\ttype ID int\n1213\t\n1214\tfunc (ID) String() string { return \"\" }\n1215\t\n1216\tfunc New() ID { return 0 }\n1217\t\n1218\t// api/api.go\n1219\tvar _ fmt.Stringer = user.New()\n1220\t```\n1221\t\n1222\t</td>\n1223\t<td>Not reported. <code>String</code> satisfies <code>fmt.Stringer</code></td>\n1224\t</tr>\n1225\t<tr>\n1226\t<td>\n1227\t\n1228\t```go\n1229\t// internal/user/user.go\n1230\ttype Record struct {\n1231\t\tID   int\n1232\t\tName string\n1233\t}\n1234\t\n1235\tfunc Dump(r Record) { fmt.Println(r) }\n1236\t```\n1237\t\n1238\t</td>\n1239\t<td>Not reported. <code>fmt</code> reads the fields through reflection</td>\n1240\t</tr>\n1241\t<tr>\n1242\t<td>\n1243\t\n1244\t```go\n1245\t// internal/user/user.go\n1246\ttype Record struct {\n1247\t\tName string `json:\"name\"`\n1248\t}\n1249\t```\n1250\t\n1251\t</td>\n1252\t<td>Not reported. A tag says a marshaller reads the struct</td>\n1253\t</tr>\n1254\t<tr>\n1255\t<td>\n1256\t\n1257\t```go\n1258\t// api/api_windows.go, excluded from this build\n1259\tvar _ = user.Format\n1260\t```\n1261\t\n1262\t</td>\n1263\t<td>Not reported. A build-excluded file that writes <code>user.Format</code> uses it</td>\n1264\t</tr>\n1265\t<tr>\n1266\t<td>\n1267\t\n1268\t```go\n1269\t// internal/user/user.go\n1270\ttype Status string\n1271\t\n1272\tconst (\n1273\t\tActive  Status = \"active\"\n1274\t\tBlocked Status = \"blocked\"\n1275\t)\n1276\t\n1277\tconst DefaultStatus Status = Active\n1278\t\n1279\t// api/api.go\n1280\tvar _ = user.Active\n1281\t```\n1282\t\n1283\t</td>\n1284\t<td>Not reported: <code>Blocked</code>.
