        0 |        0 |      0 |  1 of 10 |    1 |\n| summary → qualify   |        |        1 |         0 |        0 |      0 |  1 of 15 |    1 |\n\n</details>\n\n109 declarations are further: open, shared by default rather than by decision, so left out of the table and of the diagram.\n\nDeclarations crossed: 0 reported, 0 baselined, 30 declared. The columns above count within a pair, so they sum to more: a declaration reached from two namespaces is two rows and one finding.\n````\n\nOne row per directed edge, so a mutual pair is two rows. **`clears` is the number the decision turns on**: how many findings would go away if the two namespaces became one.\n\nBoth commands take `-test=false`. On a large package it changes the picture. In `net/http` the heaviest crossing is `export_test.go` reaching the transport internals, which is what that file is for.\n\n<details>\n<summary>The other columns, and the formats</summary>\n\n| Column | What it says |\n| --- | --- |\n| `clears` | Findings that would go away if these two namespaces merged. A declaration a third namespace also reaches survives the merge, so a heavy crossing can clear much less than it reaches |\n| `reached` | Declarations of the reached namespace this edge touches, over every declaration it holds. `12 of 19` says the second namespace holds the working parts of the first. Open crossings are counted under the table, not in the rows |\n| `declared` / `baselined` / `reported` | Declarations on this edge, by what became of each. A declaration reached from two namespaces is two rows and one finding, so these sum to more than the rule found. The line under the table gives the rule's own count, which is the survey's |\n| `saturation`, in the `Qualify` table | How much of a namespace the naming rule is unsatisfied by. Near the top, the namespace name is usually what is wrong |\n\n| `-format` | For |\n| --- | --- |\n| `markdown` *(default)* | A terminal **and** an issue or pull request. Cells are padded, so the output aligns in both. `inspect` adds a Mermaid diagram and folds the table under it |\n| `json` | An agent, and anything scripted |\n\nThe JSON carries four arrays.\n\n| Array | Holds |\n| --- | --- |\n| `edges`, `names` | One flat row each |\n| `crossings` | The fold the crossing table prints, `clears` included |\n| `namespaces` | The denominators every ratio divides by |\n\n`findings` carries the same `asked` flag the tables print a dash for. Markdown is a rendering of the same data.\n\n</details>\n\n## Adopting on an existing codebase\n\nA **baseline** records the violations a codebase already has: the analyzer's, and what [`declscope shrink`](#unexporting-what-no-importer-uses) reports. Both then report only what is new.\n\n```console\ndeclscope baseline ./...       # writes .declscope-baseline.yaml\n```\n\nThe file is found by the same upward lookup as the config, so its presence is all it takes.\n\n```yaml\npackages:\n  github.com/you/app/database:\n    boundary:\n      userRepository:\n        - normalizeEmail\n      statement:\n        - Statement.wheres\n      (core):\n        - open\n    overexported:\n      userRepository:\n        - FindUser\n```\n\n| | Spelling |\n| --- | --- |\n| A package-level declaration | `normalizeEmail`, under its file's namespace |\n| A [member](#members) | `Type.member`, under the namespace of its **type**'s file |\n| A method | `Type.method`, under the namespace of the file it is written in |\n| The [core namespace](#the-core-namespace) | `(core)` |\n\nAn entry is keyed by package, rule, namespace and declaration, never by position. It survives code moving within its file. It does **not** survive a declaration moving to another namespace, since the same use then crosses a different boundary.\n\nA baseline is regenerated, never edited.\n\n```console\ndeclscope baseline ./...\ngit diff .declscope-baseline.yaml   # the record of what was cleaned up\n```\n\n> [!TIP]\n> A regeneration records what one build configuration sees. A module that runs declscope under several `GOFLAGS=-tags=...` or `GOOS` settings keeps only the last run's entries.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Where the baseline is written</summary>\n\n```console\ndeclscope baseline [-o path] [-config path] [-merge] [packages]   # packages default to ./...\n```\n\nEach package's entries go to the file the analyzer will consult for that package.\n\n| Target | When |\n| --- | --- |\n| The baseline named by the package's nearest config file | That config has a `baseline` key |\n| The nearest existing `.declscope-baseline.yaml` above the package | No config names one |\n| A new `.declscope-baseline.yaml` in the working directory | Neither of the above exists |\n\nFor example, with a config in `internal/billing/` naming its own baseline, and a baseline already in `internal/legacy/`:\n\n```text\n.declscope-baseline.yaml               internal/user's entries\ninternal/\n├── user/user.go\n├── billing/\n│   ├── .declscope.yaml                baseline: billing-baseline.yaml\n│   ├── billing-baseline.yaml          internal/billing's entries\n│   └── billing.go\n└── legacy/\n    ├── .declscope-baseline.yaml       internal/legacy's entries\n    └── legacy.go\n```\n\n```console\n$ declscope baseline ./...\ndeclscope: recorded 1 violation(s) in .declscope-baseline.yaml\ndeclscope: recorded 1 violation(s) in internal/billing/billing-baseline.yaml\ndeclscope: recorded 1 violation(s) in internal/legacy/.declscope-baseline.yaml\n```\n\n`-o` bypasses that lookup and gathers every entry into one file.\n\nRecording `shrink`'s reports loads the whole module once more. `-shrink=false` skips it, for a module that does not run `shrink`.\n\nIf no pattern matches a package, the run stops and writes nothing, `-o` included. A pattern that matches nothing beside others that do gets a warning, as it does from `go vet`.\n\nEvery file written is regenerated **wholesale**. The existing one is never read, so a baseline that fails to parse is replaced like any other. A narrower pattern therefore **drops the entries of every package it does not load** from the files it writes:\n\n```console\n$ declscope baseline ./...           # records a and b\n$ declscope baseline ./a             # the file now holds only a\n$ declscope baseline -merge ./a      # a is regenerated, b is kept\n```\n\n`-merge` reads each file it writes first. It replaces the entries of the packages this run loaded, their test variants included, and keeps every other entry. Under `-shrink=false` it keeps `shrink`'s entries too, since the run recorded none. It also keeps them for a package `shrink` did not judge, which the run names on stderr as `shrink` does. A file that `-merge` cannot parse stops the run, and nothing is written.\n\n> [!NOTE]\n> `-merge` also keeps the entries of a package that was deleted or renamed, since no pattern loads it any more. A run over `./...` without `-merge` prunes them.\n\n> [!WARNING]\n> Some packages cannot reach the working directory by that lookup, such as one in another module. The run then **refuses** and names them, rather than recording entries nothing would find.\n\n</details>\n\n> [!TIP]\n> [`skills/declscope-adoption`](skills/declscope-adoption/SKILL.md) is a skill for an AI agent doing this work. It covers what each diagnostic shape means, and the measurement traps that produce false confidence. Its companion, [`skills/declscope-authoring`](skills/declscope-authoring/SKILL.md), is for everyday code: where a declaration goes, and how to name it accurately. The binary carries both:\n>\n> ```console\n> declscope skill install            # the agents already set up in this project\n> declscope skill install --agent claude-code --scope user\n> declscope skill list               # where they are, and whether they are current\n> ```\n>\n> Without the binary, `gh skill install mpyw/declscope declscope-authoring --agent claude-code` writes to the same directories, and the same with `declscope-adoption`. The binary's installer is [`go-skill-embed`](https://github.com/mpyw/go-skill-embed), which takes them from `gh skill install`.\n\n## Using it with an AI agent\n\ndeclscope runs wherever an agent's edits are checked.\n\n```bash\ndeclscope ./...        # in CI, and in the agent's build loop\ndeclscope -fix ./...   # deterministic: at most one fix per diagnostic\n```\n\nOn an existing codebase, run `declscope baseline ./...` once first. The agent is then shown only the boundaries its own edits cross.\n\n`declscope skill install` installs both skills. `declscope-authoring` says where a new declaration belongs, and how to name one without bending the name to pass the naming rule.\n\n| Property | Effect on the agent |\n| --- | --- |\n| The diagnostic names the namespace crossed | The agent is told why the use is wrong, and the repair is mechanical |\n| A directive is a durable record of intent | The next agent inherits the decision instead of re-deriving it |\n\nFor the work of introducing it, give the agent `-format=json` rather than the diagnostics.\n\n```bash\ndeclscope survey -format=json ./...             # what is in force, and which package to open\ndeclscope inspect -format=json ./internal/cmd   # its namespaces, crossings, edges and names\n```\n\nRank by `crossings[].clears`, and pass `-test=false` to take test scaffolding out of the ranking. The JSON keeps an agent from counting message fragments, and it refuses rather than reporting a zero for a package that did not compile.\n\n## Limits\n\ndeclscope reads one package at a time, and counts a use only where a name is written.\n\n| Not seen | Consequence |\n| --- | --- |\n| Uses outside the package | A scope beyond `shared` could not be checked, so none exists. [`declscope shrink`](#unexporting-what-no-importer-uses) loads the module to judge exportedness inside `internal/` |\n| Whole-value operations on a struct | Copying, comparing or zeroing a value names no field |\n| A composite literal of a type parameter with a `~struct` term | `P{1}` with `P interface{ ~struct{ n int } }` fills the fields of whatever `P` is instantiated with, without naming them. A struct the constraint names, as in `P interface{ Slot }` or `P interface{ ~*Slot }`, is read |\n| Reflection, `//go:linkname`, generated files | These reach a declaration without spelling it |\n| A file that imports `\"C\"` | cgo rewrites it into a generated file in the build cache. Like other generated files, it is not read: nothing in it is reported, and its uses do not count |\n| A declaration nobody uses | `boundary` needs a use to find, so unused code produces no diagnostic |\n\nFor the last row, use an unused-code linter: [`deadcode`](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/cmd/deadcode), or staticcheck's `unused` for a library with no `main` to root from.\n\n## License\n\nMIT\n","numLines":460,"startLine":1372,"totalLines":1831}},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"toolu_01WEAxkmWt86iMLS4n936iwJ","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

Read this when introducing declscope to a repository, when choosing its configuration, when running declscope shrink for the first time, or when clearing a declscope baseline. Covers sizing each rule before enabling it, reading the diagnostics as structure, the remedy for each shape, and the measurement traps that produce false confidence. For writing new code in a repository that already runs declscope, use declscope-authoring.\nlicense: MIT\nx-embedded-by: declscope\nx-embedded-version: devel\nx-embedded-at: \"2026-11-17T10:35:00Z\"\nx-embedded-digest: \"sha256:95b89ae2e7904a1bd4e000c3cb254645ae22dc91c52f1bf12a04d518dc97ea8e\"\n---\n\n# Adopting declscope\n\nWritten against **declscope 0.24.1**. Check the version first with `declscope -V=full`: this describes how that release behaves, not how an older one does.\n\n**Read [the README](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope#readme) before the first decision.** This skill covers what to do about the diagnostics. What each directive means, and what the config accepts, is there.\n\nThis skill is for introducing declscope. Placing, scoping and naming individual declarations is [declscope-authoring](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md), installed beside this one. Read it before step 3 of the [order of work](#order-of-work), and before any rename.\n\n## Check what is switched on\n\nA count of zero may mean nothing is checked. These are the defaults:\n\n| Setting | Default | |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `rules.naming.qualify` | `never` | The naming rule is **off** |\n| `rules.naming.exported` | `false` | Even when on, it skips exported declarations |\n| `rules.surplus` | `strict` | The surplus rule is **on** and judges each declaration a directive widens. `loose` judges a directive as a whole; `off` turns it off |\n| `rules.boundary` | `on` | The boundary rule is **on**. `off` stops checking reach; set `surplus: off` alongside it |\n| `rules.unused` | `strict` | The unused rule is **on**. It reports an ignore that silenced nothing, and a scope directive that restates the scope in force. `loose` reports a scope directive only when no configuration could make it bind; `off` turns it off. Malformed directives are the `directive` rule's, which is always on |\n| `filter.only` | None | When set anywhere in the chain, files outside it are never read |\n\nThe config is looked up from each analyzed package's directory **upwards**, so a subtree can carry its own and a repository can have several. Find them all, and do not read the root alone:\n\n```bash\ndeclscope survey ./...   # Checks in force: one row per config chain, with what it switched on\n```\n\nThat answers it directly. To read the files themselves:\n\n```bash\nfind . -name '.declscope.y*ml' -not -path './.git/*' \\\n  -exec sh -c 'echo \"== $1\"; cat \"$1\"' _ {} \\;\n```\n\nFinding a config is not the answer on its own. One that never sets `qualify` leaves the naming rule off, and one that sets `boundary: off` leaves off the rule this tool exists for.\n\n**The files compose, so the nearest one does not tell you what applies.** Every file between the package and the module root is read, outermost first. A nearer file owns the keys it states and inherits the rest.\n\n`filter` is the exception to that: `only` intersects down the chain and `omit` unions, so a config file can only ever shrink what is read. A root `omit` holds everywhere below it, and no nested file undoes it.\n\nEach file's patterns are read against **its own** directory, and anchor there when they hold a separator. `gen/**` in the root and the same line in a nested file name different directories. A bare name and a leading `**/` float instead, and a `..` in a pattern is an error.\n\n### Start at the default, and offer the rest\n\n**Ask before any config change**, as [declscope-authoring](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#do-not-hide-a-report) says. That includes the first config file. Wait for an answer before changing any code, too.\n\n**The minimum is no config file at all.** `boundary`, `surplus: strict` and `unused: strict` are on. They check reach and whether directives still change anything; the naming rule checks a convention. Adopting this much is a complete adoption.\n\n**Size the default `surplus` findings before changing code.** `loose` judges a `//declscope:shared` as a whole, so one reached declaration keeps the whole directive quiet. The default `strict` also reports each declaration the directive widens for nothing, and one `declscope -fix` run inserts every `//declscope:private` it asks for. If the owner wants the narrower check, set `surplus: loose` explicitly.\n\n```bash\ndeclscope survey -format=json ./... | jq .totals.surplus.found\n```\n\nAn explicit `-config` replaces the repository's own config. Copy its keys in first when measuring a different mode.\n\n**Before `-fix`, read where its `//declscope:private` directives would land.** When most of them fall under one file-level `//declscope:shared`, the file should not be shared as a whole. Delete the file's directive instead, and share the few declarations other files use. See [Directives](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#directives).\n\n**Size the default `unused` findings too.** Under `loose`, a `//declscope:private` that names the scope `defaults.unexported` gives is kept, since another default could make it bind. The default `strict` reports it, and one `declscope -fix` run deletes it. When changing `defaults.unexported`, expect reports for directives that restate the new default. If the owner wants to keep those explicit decisions, set `unused: loose`.\n\n**If the goal is a tidier codebase, offer the naming rule on top.** It is a convention. It fires where nothing is wrong, and it costs real work. Size it before offering, with a throwaway config rather than by counting message fragments:\n\n```bash\nprintf 'rules:\\n  naming:\\n    qualify: ondemand\\n    exported: true\\n' > /tmp/q.yaml\ndeclscope survey -config /tmp/q.yaml -format=json ./... | jq .totals.qualify.found\n```\n\n```yaml\nrules:\n  naming:\n    qualify: ondemand   # ask once a package holds a second namespace\n    exported: true      # reach exported names too, since inside the package they read as bare\n```\n\n| | Measured |\n| --- | --- |\n| Default, no config | Measure in the repository being adopted |\n| `qualify: ondemand` | 89 in one repository whose boundary count was zero |\n| plus `exported: true` | 1008 in a large one |\n| `qualify: always` | More again, including single-unit packages where a prefix distinguishes nothing |\n\nPut the numbers in front of the person deciding, rather than describing the settings:\n\n```bash\nfor q in never ondemand always; do\n  printf 'rules:\\n  naming:\\n    qualify: %s\\n    exported: true\\n' \"$q\" > /tmp/q.yaml\n  printf '%-9s %s\\n' \"$q\" \"$(declscope survey -config /tmp/q.yaml -format=json ./... | jq .totals.qualify.found)\"\ndone\n```\n\nSome reports will be names that spell the namespace in another form, such as `traceValue` in `tracing.go`. The message names a `rules.naming.vocabulary` key for those. Propose the entries in the same question as the naming rule, and do not count them as renames. When to list a word and when to move code instead is in [When the name spells the namespace in another form](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#when-the-name-spells-the-namespace-in-another-form).\n\nEvery count in the rest of this skill assumes `qualify: ondemand` with `exported: true`. That is what the numbers were taken under, not a recommendation.\n\n## Shrink the exported surface first\n\n**`declscope shrink` reports the exported declarations of `internal/` packages that nothing outside their package uses.** With `-fix` it unexports them. The analyzer cannot answer this: it reads one package, and any importer might use an exported name. Inside `internal/`, Go limits the importers to one directory tree, so `shrink` loads the whole module and sees every one of them.\n\nAn exported name inside `internal/` claims that another package depends on it. Where nothing does, the claim is false, and it hides the declaration from the rest of declscope. An exported declaration takes shared scope by default, so no boundary is ever reported on it. Unexported, it takes `private`, and the analyzer checks who reaches it.\n\n### Run it before the analyzer\n\n**Run `shrink`, and apply its fixes, before you work on the analyzer's reports.** A declaration it unexports becomes private to its namespace. Wherever another file of the package uses it, the analyzer then reports a boundary crossing that was not there before. Fixing in the other order means a second round.\n\nThis happened when declscope held itself to `shrink`. The fix unexported twelve declarations, and nine of them were used from other files of their package. The analyzer then needed nine `//declscope:shared` directives to state those crossings.\n\n| Step | Command |\n| --- | --- |\n| 1. Read what `shrink` reports | `declscope shrink ./...` |\n| 2. Unexport, once the owner agrees | `declscope shrink -fix ./...` |\n| 3. Confirm the build | `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` |\n| 4. Read what the analyzer now reports | `declscope ./...` |\n| 5. State or move each new crossing | See [What each shape means](#what-each-shape-means) |\n\nAsk before step 2, the same as any other change. The fix renames every identifier naming the declaration, all inside its own package, and the doc comment that opens with the name.\n\n**When the owner cannot settle `shrink` yet, baseline it.** `declscope baseline ./...` records `shrink`'s reports with the analyzer's, and `shrink` then passes on them in CI. It is the same deferral as any baseline, and [the same rules](#a-baseline-is-for-arriving-not-for-staying) apply. A repository that does not run `shrink` passes `-shrink=false`, which skips the extra load.\n\n### Reading what it reports\n\nWhat each report asks of you, and where `shrink` stands down, is in [Reading what shrink reports](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#reading-what-shrink-reports). It is not a rule the analyzer runs, so `go vet` and golangci-lint never report it.\n\n**Deleting unused code is not `shrink`'s job.** Once a declaration is unexported, staticcheck's `unused` and gopls' `unusedfunc` report it when nothing uses it. Run them after `shrink`, not before.\n\n### Keep it in CI\n\nRun it before the analyzer there too, so that a failure reads in the order it is fixed. It exits 3 when it reports anything.\n\n```yaml\n- run: declscope shrink ./...\n- run: declscope ./...\n```\n\n## The two kinds of report\n\nThe analyzer reports two things, and `shrink` a third. **Read them separately.**\n\n| Rule | What it means |\n| --- | --- |\n| `boundary` | A file reaches a declaration another file holds. A property of the code |\n| `qualify` | A name does not carry its file's namespace. A convention |\n| `overexported` | An exported name inside `internal/` that nothing outside its package uses. Only `declscope shrink` reports it, and it goes [first](#shrink-the-exported-surface-first) |\n\nBoundary first. It is the one that points at structure.\n\n## Measure before deciding\n\nA count is not a work list. Group it first. Use two commands, not `grep`.\n\n```bash\ndeclscope survey -format=json ./...           # which package to open first\ndeclscope inspect -format=json <that package> # what shape it is in\n```\n\n`-format` takes `markdown` (the default, readable in a terminal and paste-ready) or `json`. Read the JSON.\n\nAdd `-test=false` once the first pass is read. In a large package, most of what crosses is test scaffolding. `export_test.go` reaching internals is what that file is for. It sorts above the crossings worth acting on.\n\n**`survey` refuses to print a count it cannot stand behind.** It stops on a package that does not type-check, or that imports one that does not.\n\nIt reports what was in force before anything else:\n\n- which config governed which packages;\n- whether each rule was on;\n- how many entries a baseline holds.\n\nA rule that was not asked prints `-`, never `0`. That includes a rule that stood itself down. `surplus` does so for a package holding a generated, assembly or cgo file, or a build-excluded file of its own package. It does so too under `-test=false` when the package has in-package tests.\n\n`-allow-errors` continues past a package that does not compile. The `type check` row counts it, a list under the Checks table names it with its first error (or names the failing dependency and its error), and it is given no row, so nothing in the tables reads as a clean result for it.\n\nDo **not** move the baseline aside to measure: `survey` reports `baselined` as its own column, so what is suppressed and what is left are visible at once. Do not count message fragments either; the wording of a diagnostic is not an interface, and the JSON is.\n\n| What you need | Where it is |\n| --- | --- |\n| Is anything even being checked | `checks.configs[].rules`, `checks.typeCheck` |\n| Which package to open | `packages[]`, already sorted; the first row is the heaviest |\n| Is this deferred or decided | `boundary.baselined` against `boundary.declared` |\n| Which two namespaces to merge | `inspect`'s `crossings[]`, one row per ordered pair, with `clears` |\n| Where the structure is | `inspect`'s `edges[]`, one row per declaration **and reaching namespace** |\n| Where a name is wrong | `inspect`'s `names[]`, with `fixable` saying whether `-fix` would rename it |\n\n**`clears` is the number the decision turns on.** A crossing's `reached` says how much of a namespace it touches. `clears` says how many findings would go away if the two became one namespace. It is smaller whenever a third namespace reaches the same declaration. Rank the work by `clears`, not by `reached` or `uses`.\n\n**`edges[]` does not count findings.** One declaration reached from three namespaces is three rows and one finding, so the rows always outnumber `findings.boundary.reported`. Count distinct `declaration` values, or read `crossings[]`, or read the tally.\n\nAn edge's `state` (`edges[].state`) is one of six:\n\n| State | Meaning |\n| --- | --- |\n| `reported` | A finding, printed |\n| `baselined` | A finding, absorbed by the baseline |\n| `ignored` | A finding, silenced by an ignore |\n| `declared` | No finding: a `//declscope:shared` says it is shared |\n| `open` | No finding: shared because nothing says otherwise, which is most exported API |\n| `unchecked` | No finding: `rules.boundary` is `off` |\n\n**Nothing reported, much baselined and nothing declared means nobody has decided.** Such a package reads as clean under the analyzer alone. That is why `declared` is a column.\n\nBoundary violations cluster. Measured across eight repositories, one structural decision cleared between 10 and 100 entries every time. In one repository 34 of 35 sat in a single namespace.\n\n**Start where the count is concentrated, not where it is large.** The row order does not give you that. Rows are sorted by how much is undecided, which is size. Concentration is the `largest crossing` column. A package with 12 findings over 6 namespaces sorts above one with 4 in a single crossing. The second is where one decision clears the cluster.\n\n### Reading a saturation\n\n**This needs the naming rule switched on.** It is off at the default configuration. Then `qualifyTargets` is `0`, `names[]` is empty and every ratio prints `-`. Measure with the throwaway config above before reading what follows.\n\n`inspect` reports, per namespace, how many of the declarations the naming rule examines there fail it. The ratio says which thing is wrong, and the answer is rarely the rename the diagnostic suggests.\n\n| Saturation | What is wrong | The answer |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Nearly all of them | The **namespace name** | `//declscope:namespace`, or rename the file |\n| Around half | One file holding several concerns | Split the file |\n| One or two | Those declarations | Rename them |\n\nA baselined finding counts toward it: the baseline defers a decision rather than settling it, so regenerating one moves this number without a line of code changing.\n\n## What each shape means\n\n| The diagnostics say | The code is | Do this |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| File A's declarations are nearly all used from B, and nothing goes back | A is B's working parts, not a layer under it | `//declscope:namespace <B>` on A |\n| A and B reference each other both ways | One device split across two files | Give both the same namespace and rename to say so |\n| A type's fields are read from four files | One type filed by concern | The files share a namespace, or join the core |\n| Calls run one way through three files | A pipeline, and the layers are real | Keep the files. Declare only what crosses, with the reason |\n| `pkg.Foo` is asked to become `pkg.PkgFoo` | The file is the package's API | `//declscope:core` |\n| One helper is used from several files | Shared on purpose | Move it to a file named for its concept, then `//declscope:shared // why`. See [Where a new declaration goes](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#where-a-new-declaration-goes) |\n| A name reads badly with its namespace in it | Often the file name, not the declaration | Rename the file |\n\n**Two rows can fire on one cluster.** A mutual pair whose declarations four other namespaces also read matches both the second row and the third. Take the one with the larger `clears`. Merging two namespaces settles only what no third namespace reaches. So the fan-in case is usually the smaller change, and the core case the larger.\n\nThat last row is worth its own note. In one repository a single file held three concerns, and splitting it into three cleared every entry in that cluster **without renaming a single declaration**. The file name was the thing that was wrong.\n\n## Scopes and names of single declarations\n\nOnce the structure is settled, what is left is per declaration. Field scopes are in [Shared structs](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#shared-structs-private-fields), and names in [Naming](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#naming). During an adoption, one `declscope -fix` run under `surplus: strict` adds every field directive the structs need. Moving those fields to the end stays manual.\n\n## Do not turn the check off\n\n**Never set `rules.boundary: off` to reach zero.** Every count after it is meaningless. It is the repository owner's choice, for a repository that wants the ownership mark in a name without the scope behind it. It is never a step in an adoption. A baseline is one, because it records what the code already has and still reports what is new. The other shortcuts are in [Do not hide a report](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#do-not-hide-a-report).\n\nMarking every file in a package core leaves no boundary and no naming check there. What core does is in [Where a new declaration goes](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#where-a-new-declaration-goes).\n\n**Count it.** A package where every file is core needs a reason you can state in one sentence. There should be few of them.\n\n```bash\nfor d in $(find . -name '*.go' -not -name '*_test.go' | xargs -n1 dirname | sort -u); do\n  n=$(ls $d/*.go 2>/dev/null | grep -vc _test)\n  c=$(grep -l \"declscope:core\" $d/*.go 2>/dev/null | grep -vc _test)\n  [ \"$n\" = \"$c\" ] && [ \"$n\" != \"0\" ] && echo \"all core: $d\"\ndone\n```\n\nTwo of nine repositories reached zero without using `core` at all. One solved its worst cluster by promoting a file to its own package, because the file already documented itself as temporary and had one caller. A package boundary was the honest answer, and no directive could have said it.\n\n## A baseline is for arriving, not for staying\n\n`declscope baseline ./...` records what exists so that new code is held to the rule. It suppresses and does not endorse.\n\nIf the goal is zero, delete the file rather than regenerating it. An empty baseline left in the tree says nothing.\n\n## Traps\n\nThese cost real time. Each was measured, not guessed.\n\n**Measure through `declscope survey`.** Why a bare count misleads, and the bulk-rename trap, are in [Traps](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#traps).\n\n**A zero may be the filter, not the code.** A `filter.only` anywhere in the chain can leave a package with nothing to read. A package nothing was read from reports nothing. `declscope` says so only when a nested `only` was cancelled by one above it, so the quiet cases stay quiet. Fix that report in the config chain: a `//declscope:ignore filter` silences nothing, and the `unused` rule reports it. `declscope inspect` lists the files each namespace was built from (`namespaces[].files`); a package whose files are missing from it is one the filter removed.\n\n**A zero from `boundary` may be the switch, not the code.** `rules.boundary: off` silences the rule entirely, and the run looks like a clean repository. Read every config before reporting a count, the same way you would for `qualify`.\n\n**`-fix` widens**, as [declscope-authoring](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#acting-on-a-diagnostic-your-change-caused) explains. Over a whole codebase that is the wholesale widening step 3 of the order of work exists to avoid. In an adoption, use it only for renames after the structure is settled, where `names[].fixable` is true.\n\n**A dirty working tree poisons a comparison.** Measuring option A, then option B without reverting, measures A and B together. `git stash` leaves untracked files behind, so a new file from the previous attempt stays. Copy the tree instead:\n\n```bash\ncp -r repo /tmp/try-a   # and measure there\n```\n\n## Order of work\n\n1. `declscope survey ./...`, and read Checks in force before any count\n2. If the repository has `internal/` packages, run `declscope shrink ./...` and settle it before anything else. Its fixes add boundary reports, and nothing that follows adds reports back\n3. Clear `boundary` by moving the boundary, not by widening everything\n4. Re-measure with `survey`. Naming often falls with it, since merging two namespaces into one takes `ondemand` out of force\n5. Fix the file names that do not match their contents\n6. Rename what is left, following [Naming](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#naming)\n7. Delete the baseline\n8. Check the core count, and `go vet`, `go test`, `declscope shrink` and `declscope` in that order","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"c2b8ba51-0db5-4d81-afe9-4988cb71a59c","uuid":"0b7d3bc0-bbbb-4d24-bb50-ef64d11e12ca","timestamp":"2026-11-17T10:35:02.222Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"---\nname: declscope-adoption\ndescription: Adopt declscope on an existing Go codebase and drive its diagnostics to zero. Unexport, once the owner agrees | `declscope shrink -fix ./...` |\n| 3. Confirm the build | `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` |\n| 4. Read what the analyzer now reports | `declscope ./...` |\n| 5. State or move each new crossing | See [What each shape means](#what-each-shape-means) |\n\nAsk before step 2, the same as any other change. The fix renames every identifier naming the declaration, all inside its own package, and the doc comment that opens with the name.\n\n**When the owner cannot settle `shrink` yet, baseline it.** `declscope baseline ./...` records `shrink`'s reports with the analyzer's, and `shrink` then passes on them in CI. It is the same deferral as any baseline, and [the same rules](#a-baseline-is-for-arriving-not-for-staying) apply. A repository that does not run `shrink` passes `-shrink=false`, which skips the extra load.\n\n### Reading what it reports\n\nWhat each report asks of you, and where `shrink` stands down, is in [Reading what shrink reports](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#reading-what-shrink-reports). It is not a rule the analyzer runs, so `go vet` and golangci-lint never report it.\n\n**Deleting unused code is not `shrink`'s job.** Once a declaration is unexported, staticcheck's `unused` and gopls' `unusedfunc` report it when nothing uses it. Run them after `shrink`, not before.\n\n### Keep it in CI\n\nRun it before the analyzer there too, so that a failure reads in the order it is fixed. It exits 3 when it reports anything.\n\n```yaml\n- run: declscope shrink ./...\n- run: declscope ./...\n```\n\n## The two kinds of report\n\nThe analyzer reports two things, and `shrink` a third. **Read them separately.**\n\n| Rule | What it means |\n| --- | --- |\n| `boundary` | A file reaches a declaration another file holds. A property of the code |\n| `qualify` | A name does not carry its file's namespace. A convention |\n| `overexported` | An exported name inside `internal/` that nothing outside its package uses. Only `declscope shrink` reports it, and it goes [first](#shrink-the-exported-surface-first) |\n\nBoundary first. It is the one that points at structure.\n\n## Measure before deciding\n\nA count is not a work list. Group it first. Use two commands, not `grep`.\n\n```bash\ndeclscope survey -format=json ./...           # which package to open first\ndeclscope inspect -format=json <that package> # what shape it is in\n```\n\n`-format` takes `markdown` (the default, readable in a terminal and paste-ready) or `json`. Read the JSON.\n\nAdd `-test=false` once the first pass is read. In a large package, most of what crosses is test scaffolding. `export_test.go` reaching internals is what that file is for. It sorts above the crossings worth acting on.\n\n**`survey` refuses to print a count it cannot stand behind.** It stops on a package that does not type-check, or that imports one that does not.\n\nIt reports what was in force before anything else:\n\n- which config governed which packages;\n- whether each rule was on;\n- how many entries a baseline holds.\n\nA rule that was not asked prints `-`, never `0`. That includes a rule that stood itself down. `surplus` does so for a package holding a generated, assembly or cgo file, or a build-excluded file of its own package. It does so too under `-test=false` when the package has in-package tests.\n\n`-allow-errors` continues past a package that does not compile. The `type check` row counts it, a list under the Checks table names it with its first error (or names the failing dependency and its error), and it is given no row, so nothing in the tables reads as a clean result for it.\n\nDo **not** move the baseline aside to measure: `survey` reports `baselined` as its own column, so what is suppressed and what is left are visible at once. Do not count message fragments either; the wording of a diagnostic is not an interface, and the JSON is.\n\n| What you need | Where it is |\n| --- | --- |\n| Is anything even being checked | `checks.configs[].rules`, `checks.typeCheck` |\n| Which package to open | `packages[]`, already sorted; the first row is the heaviest |\n| Is this deferred or decided | `boundary.baselined` against `boundary.declared` |\n| Which two namespaces to merge | `inspect`'s `crossings[]`, one row per ordered pair, with `clears` |\n| Where the structure is | `inspect`'s `edges[]`, one row per declaration **and reaching namespace** |\n| Where a name is wrong | `inspect`'s `names[]`, with `fixable` saying whether `-fix` would rename it |\n\n**`clears` is the number the decision turns on.** A crossing's `reached` says how much of a namespace it touches. `clears` says how many findings would go away if the two became one namespace. It is smaller whenever a third namespace reaches the same declaration. Rank the work by `clears`, not by `reached` or `uses`.\n\n**`edges[]` does not count findings.** One declaration reached from three namespaces is three rows and one finding, so the rows always outnumber `findings.boundary.reported`. Count distinct `declaration` values, or read `crossings[]`, or read the tally.\n\nAn edge's `state` (`edges[].state`) is one of six:\n\n| State | Meaning |\n| --- | --- |\n| `reported` | A finding, printed |\n| `baselined` | A finding, absorbed by the baseline |\n| `ignored` | A finding, silenced by an ignore |\n| `declared` | No finding: a `//declscope:shared` says it is shared |\n| `open` | No finding: shared because nothing says otherwise, which is most exported API |\n| `unchecked` | No finding: `rules.boundary` is `off` |\n\n**Nothing reported, much baselined and nothing declared means nobody has decided.** Such a package reads as clean under the analyzer alone. That is why `declared` is a column.\n\nBoundary violations cluster. Measured across eight repositories, one structural decision cleared between 10 and 100 entries every time. In one repository 34 of 35 sat in a single namespace.\n\n**Start where the count is concentrated, not where it is large.** The row order does not give you that. Rows are sorted by how much is undecided, which is size. Concentration is the `largest crossing` column. A package with 12 findings over 6 namespaces sorts above one with 4 in a single crossing. The second is where one decision clears the cluster.\n\n### Reading a saturation\n\n**This needs the naming rule switched on.** It is off at the default configuration. Then `qualifyTargets` is `0`, `names[]` is empty and every ratio prints `-`. Measure with the throwaway config above before reading what follows.\n\n`inspect` reports, per namespace, how many of the declarations the naming rule examines there fail it. The ratio says which thing is wrong, and the answer is rarely the rename the diagnostic suggests.\n\n| Saturation | What is wrong | The answer |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Nearly all of them | The **namespace name** | `//declscope:namespace`, or rename the file |\n| Around half | One file holding several concerns | Split the file |\n| One or two | Those declarations | Rename them |\n\nA baselined finding counts toward it: the baseline defers a decision rather than settling it, so regenerating one moves this number without a line of code changing.\n\n## What each shape means\n\n| The diagnostics say | The code is | Do this |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| File A's declarations are nearly all used from B, and nothing goes back | A is B's working parts, not a layer under it | `//declscope:namespace <B>` on A |\n| A and B reference each other both ways | One device split across two files | Give both the same namespace and rename to say so |\n| A type's fields are read from four files | One type filed by concern | The files share a namespace, or join the core |\n| Calls run one way through three files | A pipeline, and the layers are real | Keep the files. Declare only what crosses, with the reason |\n| `pkg.Foo` is asked to become `pkg.PkgFoo` | The file is the package's API | `//declscope:core` |\n| One helper is used from several files | Shared on purpose | Move it to a file named for its concept, then `//declscope:shared // why`. See [Where a new declaration goes](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#where-a-new-declaration-goes) |\n| A name reads badly with its namespace in it | Often the file name, not the declaration | Rename the file |\n\n**Two rows can fire on one cluster.** A mutual pair whose declarations four other namespaces also read matches both the second row and the third. Take the one with the larger `clears`. Merging two namespaces settles only what no third namespace reaches. So the fan-in case is usually the smaller change, and the core case the larger.\n\nThat last row is worth its own note. In one repository a single file held three concerns, and splitting it into three cleared every entry in that cluster **without renaming a single declaration**. The file name was the thing that was wrong.\n\n## Scopes and names of single declarations\n\nOnce the structure is settled, what is left is per declaration. Field scopes are in [Shared structs](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#shared-structs-private-fields), and names in [Naming](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#naming). During an adoption, one `declscope -fix` run under `surplus: strict` adds every field directive the structs need. Moving those fields to the end stays manual.\n\n## Do not turn the check off\n\n**Never set `rules.boundary: off` to reach zero.** Every count after it is meaningless. It is the repository owner's choice, for a repository that wants the ownership mark in a name without the scope behind it. It is never a step in an adoption. A baseline is one, because it records what the code already has and still reports what is new. The other shortcuts are in [Do not hide a report](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#do-not-hide-a-report).\n\nMarking every file in a package core leaves no boundary and no naming check there. What core does is in [Where a new declaration goes](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#where-a-new-declaration-goes).\n\n**Count it.** A package where every file is core needs a reason you can state in one sentence. There should be few of them.\n\n```bash\nfor d in $(find . -name '*.go' -not -name '*_test.go' | xargs -n1 dirname | sort -u); do\n  n=$(ls $d/*.go 2>/dev/null | grep -vc _test)\n  c=$(grep -l \"declscope:core\" $d/*.go 2>/dev/null | grep -vc _test)\n  [ \"$n\" = \"$c\" ] && [ \"$n\" != \"0\" ] && echo \"all core: $d\"\ndone\n```\n\nTwo of nine repositories reached zero without using `core` at all. One solved its worst cluster by promoting a file to its own package, because the file already documented itself as temporary and had one caller. A package boundary was the honest answer, and no directive could have said it.\n\n## A baseline is for arriving, not for staying\n\n`declscope baseline ./...` records what exists so that new code is held to the rule. It suppresses and does not endorse.\n\nIf the goal is zero, delete the file rather than regenerating it. An empty baseline left in the tree says nothing.\n\n## Traps\n\nThese cost real time. Each was measured, not guessed.\n\n**Measure through `declscope survey`.** Why a bare count misleads, and the bulk-rename trap, are in [Traps](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#traps).\n\n**A zero may be the filter, not the code.** A `filter.only` anywhere in the chain can leave a package with nothing to read. A package nothing was read from reports nothing. `declscope` says so only when a nested `only` was cancelled by one above it, so the quiet cases stay quiet. Fix that report in the config chain: a `//declscope:ignore filter` silences nothing, and the `unused` rule reports it. `declscope inspect` lists the files each namespace was built from (`namespaces[].files`); a package whose files are missing from it is one the filter removed.\n\n**A zero from `boundary` may be the switch, not the code.** `rules.boundary: off` silences the rule entirely, and the run looks like a clean repository. Read every config before reporting a count, the same way you would for `qualify`.\n\n**`-fix` widens**, as [declscope-authoring](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#acting-on-a-diagnostic-your-change-caused) explains. Over a whole codebase that is the wholesale widening step 3 of the order of work exists to avoid. In an adoption, use it only for renames after the structure is settled, where `names[].fixable` is true.\n\n**A dirty working tree poisons a comparison.** Measuring option A, then option B without reverting, measures A and B together. `git stash` leaves untracked files behind, so a new file from the previous attempt stays. Copy the tree instead:\n\n```bash\ncp -r repo /tmp/try-a   # and measure there\n```\n\n## Order of work\n\n1. `declscope survey ./...`, and read Checks in force before any count\n2. If the repository has `internal/` packages, run `declscope shrink ./...` and settle it before anything else. Its fixes add boundary reports, and nothing that follows adds reports back\n3. Clear `boundary` by moving the boundary, not by widening everything\n4. Re-measure with `survey`. Naming often falls with it, since merging two namespaces into one takes `ondemand` out of force\n5. Fix the file names that do not match their contents\n6. Rename what is left, following [Naming](../declscope-authoring/SKILL.md#naming)\n7. Delete the baseline\n8. Check the version first with `declscope -V=full`: this describes how that release behaves, not how an older one does.\n\nThis skill is for everyday work in a repository that already runs declscope. Introducing it, choosing its configuration, and clearing a baseline are in [declscope-adoption](../declscope-adoption/SKILL.md), installed beside this one. What each directive and config key means is in [the README](https://github.com/mpyw/declscope#readme).\n\n## The model\n\nA file is a namespace. Its name comes from the file name: `user_repository.go` is `userRepository`. A `//declscope:namespace` above the package clause names it instead.\n\n| Declaration | Scope by default | Who may use it |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Unexported | `private` | Its own namespace only |\n| Exported | `shared` | Any file of the package |\n| With `//declscope:shared`, or in a file with one above the package clause | `shared` | Any file of the package |\n| With `//declscope:private`, or in a file with one above the package clause | `private` | Its own namespace only |\n\n**A field or an interface method takes the nearest scope stated for it.** The order is its own directive, its type's, a file-level one, then the default. With nothing stated, an unexported field of an exported type is private.\n\nA method is not a member. It belongs to the file it is written in, and a directive on its type does not reach it.\n\nWhich rules are on, and which config governs a package, is in [Check what is switched on](../declscope-adoption/SKILL.md#check-what-is-switched-on). Read \"Checks in force\" from `declscope survey ./...` before trusting a count.\n\n**A count of zero may mean nothing is checked.** The naming rule is off unless a config turns it on. Under `qualify: ondemand` it applies once a package has a second namespace. It skips exported names unless `rules.naming.exported` is on.\n\n## Where a new declaration goes\n\n**Put it in the file whose concern it is.** That choice decides its namespace, so it decides who may use it and what its name must carry. The directive and the name follow from it.\n\n| The declaration is used by | Put it | Scope |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Code in one file | That file | Default. No directive |\n| Several files, as a shared helper on purpose | A file named for its concept, not the file of its first caller | `//declscope:shared // <who uses it and why>`. A file-level one only when the file is shared by nature. See [Directives](#directives) |\n| Most files of the package, as its shared model | A core file: `//declscope:core` plus a file-level `//declscope:shared` | Package-wide, from the file directive |\n| Another package | Wherever it belongs, exported | Default for exported names |\n\n**A core file does not share its declarations by itself.** `//declscope:core` sets only the namespace, and exempts the file from the naming rule. Its unexported declarations are still private to the core. A core file whose declarations are shared also needs a file-level `//declscope:shared`.\n\n**Before widening, ask whether the code is in the wrong file.** A boundary report on your new use says a file reached into another namespace. Often the function you are writing belongs beside what it uses. When the declaration is shared on purpose, check that it sits in a file named for its concept before you write the directive.\n\n**Do not create a file just to satisfy a name.** A new twenty-line file holding one declaration that only its old file uses is a warning sign. Rename the declaration where it was. A declaration that several parts share is different: move it, as the table above says.\n\n## Common changes\n\n| Change | What declscope does | Do this |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Add a method to a type, in another file | The method takes its own file's namespace. Each private field it reads is reported at the field, in the type's file | Put the method in the type's file. If the two files are one unit, give the method's file the type's namespace with `//declscope:namespace`. Do not widen the fields |\n| Add a field that another file reads | Under a `//declscope:shared` type it is shared already. With nothing stated, the use is reported | When the type is unexported and other files spell it, write `//declscope:shared` on the type. See [Shared structs: private fields](#shared-structs-private-fields). Otherwise, exported types included, write `//declscope:shared // <who reads it>` on each field that is read, however many there are |\n| Move code between files | Its namespace changes, and so does the name it must carry | Rename it, move its tests with it, and reread each `// reason` that names a file |\n| Split a file | Each new file is a new namespace, so calls between the halves are reported | Split along a real boundary. If the halves are one unit, give them one `//declscope:namespace` |\n| Export a name to get past a report | An exported name takes shared scope, so the report goes away | Do not. In `internal/`, `declscope shrink` reports it. Elsewhere it becomes public API |\n| Add a helper used only by generated code | Generated files are not read. The `surplus` rule stands down in a package holding one, so nothing is reported | Nothing to write. Never put directives in generated files, since they are not read. An ignore would silence nothing |\n\n## Naming\n\nThis applies when the naming rule is on. The namespace may sit anywhere in the name, but it must start a word. Its right edge may fall inside a word: `loadUserID` carries `user`, and `poweruserID` does not.\n\nFields, interface methods, and methods written in their type's file are exempt. A method in another file must carry that file's namespace. So do helpers in a test file. `TestXxx`, `BenchmarkXxx`, `FuzzXxx` and `ExampleXxx` in a `_test.go` file are exempt, since `go test` finds them by name.\n\n**Prefer natural word order.** With a verb namespace, a prefix reads as a command: `collectAddFunc` is an instruction, and `addFuncToCollection` is a name. An entry point is the exception, since `collectFiles` already says what it does.\n\n**A verb prefix can promise a side effect the code does not have.** A name that starts with a verb reads as that action. In `delete.go`, a function that only checks whether a user may be deleted must not be called `deleteUser`. A reader expects it to delete the user. Name it for what it does, and fit the namespace in elsewhere: `canDeleteUser`, `usersToDelete`. Keep the verb first only for code that performs the action.\n\nA verb file name is still fine. Its regular noun and past forms often carry it already, since the namespace's right edge may fall inside a word. In `collect.go`, `collectedFiles`, `collectionKeys` and `addToCollection` all carry `collect`. A form that changes the verb's spelling, such as `deletion` for `delete`, needs another fit or a vocabulary entry. The two generated forms are the exception. See [When the name spells the namespace in another form](#when-the-name-spells-the-namespace-in-another-form).\n\n### Fitting the namespace in\n\nA prefix is one fit, and often the right one: `userProfile` is a prefix. Do not use it by reflex, though. Choose the place where the namespace reads as part of the phrase:\n\n| Fit it in as | Namespace | Examples |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| A modifier before a noun | `user` | `userProfile`, `userRow` |\n| The object after a verb | `user` | `loadUser`, `deleteUserByID` |\n| A phrase after the main word | `collect` | `addFuncToCollection` |\n| An inflected form | `collect`, `store` | `collectedFiles`, `storingKeys`, `storedKeys` |\n| A word it begins, ending inside it | `parse` | `SpecifierParser` |\n\n**Then read the name aloud.** A command (`collectAddFunc`), a stack of nouns with no grammar, or a word used against its meaning means another fit is needed. When no fit reads naturally, the name is not the problem. Suspect the file instead: see [An ill-fitting prefix means the declaration is in the wrong file](#an-ill-fitting-prefix-means-the-declaration-is-in-the-wrong-file).\n\n### Carrying the namespace does not make a name accurate\n\nThe rule checks that the namespace is in the name. It cannot check that the rest of the name is true. Name the declaration for exactly what it is, then make sure the namespace is in it. Before naming a collection, read the code that fills it.\n\n| Written | Wrong because | Better |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `methodNames`, filled with every function | Plain functions are in it too, not only methods | `funcNames`, or fill it with methods only |\n| `collectInfo` | The namespace is the only real word, so the name says nothing | Name what it holds: `collectedFiles` |\n| `orderSortKeys` in `order.go`, read by every file | The prefix claims one owner | Move it. See the next section |\n\nWhen the accurate name reads badly with the namespace in it, do not bend the words. Read it as a signal about placement.\n\n### An ill-fitting prefix means the declaration is in the wrong file\n\nSometimes the namespace a name must carry does not describe the thing. Then the declaration sits in the wrong file, and renaming it hides that.\n\nFor example, a cache that two parts of a package read was placed in `surplus.go`. So it had to be called `surplusLinknamed`, and the other part's call read `c.surplusLinknamed(pass)`, as if it asked the surplus code. It belonged in the package's shared-model file, which is core and shared as a whole. There it is just `linknamed`.\n\n| The prefix you must add | Do this |\n| --- | --- |\n| Describes what the thing is | Keep it |\n| Belongs to one caller, but several parts use the thing | Move it to a file named for its concept, or to the shared-model file. A concept file often carries the name for free: `linknamed` carries `linkname` |\n| Reads badly for most names in the file | Often the file name is wrong. See [What each shape means](../declscope-adoption/SKILL.md#what-each-shape-means) |\n\n### Name a test file for the code it calls\n\nA test file's namespace comes from its own file name: `collect_test.go` is `collect`. So name a test file for the source file whose unexported code it calls, not for the behavior it tests. A test of ordering that calls `collect.go` goes in `collect_test.go`, not `order_test.go`.\n\nThe namespace does not follow the subject's `//declscope:namespace`. If `user_extra.go` carries `//declscope:namespace user`, write the same directive on `user_extra_test.go`. A test of a core file joins the core by itself: `client_test.go` joins a core `client.go`. Nothing else joins, so the core takes no GOOS sibling such as `client_linux.go`. A test file with its own `//declscope:namespace` keeps that namespace instead.\n\n| The test calls | Put it |\n| --- | --- |\n| Unexported code of one file | That file's `_test.go` |\n| Unexported code of two files | Split the test, or test through a shared entry point |\n| A helper shared by several test files | A test file named for the helper, such as `fixture_test.go`. Put `//declscope:shared // <which tests use it>` on the helper |\n| Only exported names | Anywhere, including `package x_test` |\n\n**Uses only in `_test.go` files mean the test is misplaced.** Move the test. Never widen production code for a test, and never let `-fix` insert `//declscope:shared` for one.\n\n### When the name spells the namespace in another form\n\nOnly the namespace's own spelling and two generated forms carry it: a final `e` dropped before `ing` (`store` → `storing`) and `y` turned to `i` (`apply` → `applies`, `applied`). Generation only makes the namespace longer. Nothing else is guessed:\n\n| File | Name | Carried | Why |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| `store.go` | `storingKeys` | Yes | A generated form |\n| `tracing.go` | `traceValue`, `tracerType` | No | The stem of an inflected file name is not derived |\n| `walking.go` | `walkSpeed` | No | Same |\n| `index.go` | `indicesSorted` | No | An irregular form |\n\n**Prefer the base form of a word for a new file name.** It is a recommendation, not a requirement. `trace.go` is carried by `traceValue`, `tracerType` and `tracingStart`. `tracing.go` is carried only by the last. Generated forms and the free right edge both run from the namespace to longer words, so the base form reaches every form the inflected file name reaches, and more. The same holds for `entry.go` over `entries.go`, `walk.go` over `walking.go`, and `user.go` over `users.go`. An inflected file name is allowed. It only fits declscope worse, so choose it when it reads clearly better.\n\nFor an existing file, renaming it to the base form keeps every name that carried the old namespace. It still changes the namespace, so it is not free: rename its test files too, and update any `//declscope:namespace` that names it, baseline entries keyed by it, and each `// reason` that names the file. Do not rename an existing file only for this. Mention the rename as an option. When it is too wide, or the owner prefers the current name, a vocabulary entry is the smaller change.\n\n`rules.naming.vocabulary` lists extra words that carry a namespace. A listed word goes through the same test as the namespace, so `trace` also covers `tracer`. When the namespace looks inflected, the diagnostic names the key: `list that form under rules.naming.vocabulary.tracing`.\n\n```yaml\nrules:\n  naming:\n    vocabulary:\n      tracing: [trace]\n      index: [indices]\n```\n\nUse it for a word that names what the namespace names: another form of it, or the domain's word for part of it (`mouse: [wheel]`). For those, the rename the message offers would stutter (`tracingTraceValue`).\n\n| The name | Do this |\n| --- | --- |\n| Spells the base form of an inflected file name | Propose a vocabulary entry, and mention renaming the file to the base form as an option |\n| Spells the namespace in another form the base form cannot reach (`indices`), or the domain's word for part of it | Propose a vocabulary entry |\n| Spells a different word, which describes the thing better | The file may be named wrong, or the declaration may be in the wrong file. See [An ill-fitting prefix](#an-ill-fitting-prefix-means-the-declaration-is-in-the-wrong-file) |\n| Would need a long list of words | Split the file. A long list means the file declares things it is not about |\n\nA vocabulary entry is a config change, so ask first. List the word the name actually spells. Do not list a stem you guessed: `trac` would also carry `track`.\n\n## Directives\n\nOnly the exact form `//declscope:name` is a directive: a line comment, no space after the slashes or the colon. Anything else starting with `declscope:` is reported as malformed.\n\n| Directive | Where it goes | Note |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `//declscope:shared`, `//declscope:private` | The doc comment of the declaration, or trailing its first or last line | On a block, it reaches every spec in it |\n| The same, file-level | Above the package clause | Reaches every declaration in the file, members included |\n| `//declscope:ignore <rules>` | The same places as either of the above. Rules are comma-separated | A bare ignore silences every rule except `overexported` |\n| `//declscope:namespace <name>` | Above the package clause | Below it, the `directive` rule reports it, and it has no effect |\n| `//declscope:core` | Above the package clause | Sets the namespace only. It shares nothing |\n\n**Write the reason after `//`.** `//declscope:shared // rename.go reads it` and `//declscope:ignore boundary // why` are directives with reasons. Any other text after the name is read as an argument. `//declscope:ignore boundary because ...` is reported as an unknown rule.\n\n**A directive records a decision.** Write one only when it changes something, and say why. Under the default `unused: strict`, a directive that restates the scope already in force is reported.\n\n**Share a whole file only when the file exists to be shared.** A directive on a file or a block reaches everything inside it. Each exception then needs a directive of its own. A file-level `//declscope:shared` also makes every new declaration in the file start shared. So it should describe what the file is, not who happens to use it today.\n\n| The file or block | Write |\n| --- | --- |\n| Is shared by nature, such as a utility file or the package's shared model, and a few declarations are its internals | `//declscope:shared` on the whole, and `//declscope:private` on each of the few internals |\n| Happens to have many declarations used from other files right now | `//declscope:shared` on each of them, and nothing on the whole |\n| Has only a few declarations used from other files | `//declscope:shared` on each of those few, and nothing on the whole |\n\nDo not share a whole file to share a few declarations, then mark the rest `//declscope:private`. The file then states the opposite of what it is. A type is decided differently. An unexported type gets the directive when other files spell it, not by how many of its fields cross. An exported type is shared already, so it gets none. See [Shared structs: private fields](#shared-structs-private-fields).\n\n## Shared structs: private fields\n\nWhen another namespace uses a struct, give each field the smallest scope it needs.\n\n| Declaration | Directive |\n| --- | --- |\n| An unexported struct type, spelled from another namespace | `//declscope:shared`. Its fields inherit it |\n| An exported struct type | None. It is shared already. Its unexported fields stay private, unless a file-level directive says otherwise |\n| A field no other namespace reads, under a `//declscope:shared` type | `//declscope:private`, after its doc comment and a `//` line |\n| A field another namespace reads, under a `//declscope:shared` type | None |\n| A field another namespace reads, under any other type | `//declscope:shared // <who reads it>` |\n| An embedded field | None. It is not a target, and a directive there is reported as unused |\n\n**Do not restate the type's scope on a field.** It binds nothing and is reported as unused.\n\n**Put the private fields last,** as [Order by reach](#order-by-reach) says. The fields other files read are the struct's interface, so they come first:\n\n```go\n// callee is a resolved call target.\n//\n//declscope:shared\ntype callee struct {\n\t// obj is the declared function or method, when there is one.\n\tobj *types.Func\n\t// inputs are the values passed.\n\tinputs []ssa.Value\n\t// fn is the function called, when it is known statically.\n\t//\n\t//declscope:private\n\tfn *ssa.Function\n}\n```\n\nUnder a `//declscope:shared` type with `surplus: strict`, declscope reports each field no other namespace reads. Where `surplus` is off or stands down, find them by hand. Mark every field `//declscope:private`. Then delete the directive from each field reported as used from another namespace.\n\n**A type nobody else spells needs no directive,** even when other files read its fields. Callers that only get it from a constructor do not spell it. Keep the type private. Write `//declscope:shared // <who reads it>` on each field that another file reads, and nothing on the rest.\n\nWhen no other file reads its fields either, `//declscope:shared` on the type is reported:\n\n```text\n//declscope:shared on hidden, hidden.a: no use from another namespace is visible to declscope\n```\n\n## Order by reach\n\n**Order declarations from the widest reach to the narrowest.** A reader meets the file's interface first: what other packages use, then what other files use, then how it works. declscope does not check this order. It is a convention for code you write.\n\n| Reach | Declarations |\n| --- | --- |\n| 1. Other packages | Exported, and not `private` |\n| 2. Other files of the package | Unexported, and `shared` by any directive in force: its own, its block's, its type's or the file's |\n| 3. Its own namespace | `private`, exported or not |\n\nScope decides the reach, not the case of the first letter. An exported declaration marked `//declscope:private` goes with the private ones, since its author said no other file uses it.\n\n**Order only inside a sequence the file already has.** Keep the order of kinds. Within each reach, keep the existing order, so declarations that sit together stay together.\n\n**A type and the constructors and methods right after it are one unit.** Move the unit as a whole, at the type's reach. Do not move the type out alone, and do not move another declaration into the unit. Inside it, the type comes first, then its constructors, then its methods, each ordered by reach.\n\n| Sequence | Order by reach |\n| --- | --- |\n| The fields of a struct, the methods of an interface | Yes |\n| A run of adjacent declarations of one kind, such as consecutive functions or one `const` block | Yes |\n| A run of type units | Yes, each unit as a whole |\n| The constructors of a unit, and separately its methods | Yes, inside the unit |\n| Declarations of different kinds | No. Do not move a declaration past one of another kind |\n| Sections marked by a comment, such as `// ===` or `// Param Types` | No. Order inside each section |\n\n**A private helper may stay right after its users.** When the declarations that use it sit next to each other, put it directly after the last of them, or after another helper already placed there. Reading from the top then follows the calls. A helper whose users are spread through the file goes in reach order.\n\n```go\nfunc Resolve(dir, explicit string) (Options, error) { ... }\n\nfunc ResolveForBaseline(dir, explicit string) (Options, string, error) { ... }\n\n// resolve is used only by the two above, so it stays after them.\nfunc resolve(dir, explicit string) (Options, string, error) { ... }\n\nfunc Find(dir string) string { ... }\n```\n\nFields have no such exception. A private field goes after the shared ones, even the field the struct is built around.\n\nDo not reorder where the order is observable:\n\n| Order is observable through | Effect |\n| --- | --- |\n| `iota`, or a `const` spec with its expression omitted | Each value follows its position |\n| Unkeyed composite literals | `callee{f, in, fn}` binds fields by position |\n| Positional or binary encodings | The wire format follows the field order |\n| `unsafe` offsets | `unsafe.Offsetof` changes |\n| 64-bit atomics | They rely on first-word alignment on 32-bit platforms |\n| Package-level `var` initializers with side effects and no dependencies between them | They run in declaration order |\n| Several `init` functions in one file | They run in source order |\n\n**Keep an order the reader relies on.** Some orders change nothing for the compiler but still say something. Keep these as you would an observable order:\n\n- Steps listed in the order they run.\n- Values that follow an outside order, such as a page's layout or a protocol's fields.\n- A comment that introduces the declarations after it. Move it with them, or leave the group in place.\n\nWhen you are unsure, leave the sequence and say so in your report.\n\nWhere the repository's linters fix an order, such as `decorder` or `funcorder`, follow them first. `funcorder`'s exported-before-unexported methods is the same direction, so order by reach inside it.\n\nTest files and generated files are out of scope. `TestXxx` functions are exported but called by nobody.\n\n**When your change moves a declaration to another reach, move the declaration too.** That is the default, for a new `//declscope:shared`, a `//declscope:private` from `surplus`, or a name `shrink` unexported. Say in your report that you moved it: the move makes the diff larger, and the owner may prefer it in place. Do not reorder declarations your change does not touch.\n\n## Acting on a diagnostic your change caused\n\n**A boundary report points at the declaration you reached, not at your code.** Your use is listed under it as `used here, in namespace ...`. A directive or an ignore that answers it goes on the declaration.\n\n| Report | First question | Usual answer |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `X is private to namespace \"a\"` (or `to the core namespace`), `but is used from namespace \"b\"`, or `X is declared private by ...` | Should your code live beside `X`? | Move your code beside `X`. If `X` is shared on purpose and sits in one caller's file, move it to a file named for its concept first. Then write `//declscope:shared // why` on `X`. When `X` states its own `//declscope:private`, that was a decision: move your code, and do not flip the directive |\n| `//declscope:shared on X: no use from another namespace is visible` | Did the use that justified it go away? | Delete the directive |\n| `X takes shared scope from ..., but no use ...` | Does any other file read `X`? | Accept `-fix`'s `//declscope:private` on `X`. Move `X` after the declarations of wider reach. See [Order by reach](#order-by-reach). When the directive is a file's or a block's, and most of its declarations get this report, it should not share the whole. Delete it, and write `//declscope:shared` on the few that other files use |\n| `unused //declscope:...` | Does the directive still change anything? | Delete it |\n| `X does not carry namespace \"a\"` | Is the name accurate, and is `X` in the right file? | See [Naming](#naming). Rename only when both answers are yes |\n| `X is exported, but nothing outside ... uses it` (`declscope shrink`) | Does another package really need it? | See [Reading what shrink reports](#reading-what-shrink-reports) |\n\n**`-fix` widens. It does not draw boundaries.** On a boundary report, `-fix` inserts `//declscope:shared` instead of moving code. That also leaves the declaration in its first caller's file, with that caller's prefix. Read `-fix -diff` before `-fix`. Its rename is offered only when it is proven safe, but it cannot tell whether the name was accurate.\n\n### Reading what shrink reports\n\n`declscope shrink` reports exported declarations of `internal/` packages that nothing outside their package uses. It is a subcommand, not a rule the analyzer runs, so a clean `declscope ./...` says nothing about it.\n\n| Report | What to do |\n| --- | --- |\n| `... uses it` and nothing more | The fix is offered. Apply it with `declscope shrink -fix <that package>` |\n| `... (no fix: <reason>)` | A use may exist that `shrink` cannot prove, or the rename is unsafe. **Do not unexport it by hand.** Read the reason first |\n| `... only the external tests of <pkg> use it` | Keep it exported. Add `//declscope:ignore overexported // <why>` when the tests use it on purpose |\n| `... (no fix: a build-excluded file of another package may use it)`, where that file uses it under another build tag | Keep it exported. Add `//declscope:ignore overexported // <file, behind which tag>`. One ignore passes every configuration |\n| `declscope shrink: not judged: <pkg>: <reason>` on stderr | That package was not checked. It is not clean |\n| `declscope shrink: warning: \"<pattern>\" matched no packages` on stderr | The pattern checked nothing. Fix the pattern, as you would for `go vet` |\n| `declscope shrink: not judged: <n> package(s) outside the main module` on stderr | The patterns named packages `shrink` never judges, such as `std`. Nothing to do |\n\n**A package not judged is not a package with nothing to report.** `shrink` stands down wherever an importer could be unseen:\n\n- outside `internal/`, and in `package main`;\n- beside assembly or cgo;\n- under an `internal/` whose tree a nested module may import into, when that module fails to load or reads this one from elsewhere, such as a published version;\n- under an `internal/` whose tree a module of the build list may import into, when the build reads that module from elsewhere, such as a published version.\n\nA copy from elsewhere that a nested module builds keeps the reports in its range, but withholds their fixes, and the reason names the copy.\n\nThe exit status ignores those packages.\n\n**The values of an enum are judged as one set.** A `const` block of 2 or more constants, all of one exported type of the package, is a set. While the type is not reported, or another package uses any of its values, no value is reported. Otherwise every value is reported with the type, and is fixed only where all of them are. A constant of the type outside such a block, such as a lone default, is judged on its own. To keep it with the set, put it in the block. A report on a block that mixes in another constant says to split the block. Do not add an ignore per value.\n\nA bare `//declscope:ignore` does not reach `overexported`. Name the rule. Names written as strings, such as a template field or `reflect.Value.MethodByName`, are outside what `shrink` can see. When no interface carries the value there, add the ignore with the reason.\n\n## Do not hide a report\n\n| Tempting | Why not |\n| --- | --- |\n| `rules.boundary: off` | Turns off the rule the tool exists for |\n| `//declscope:core`, or a file-level `//declscope:shared` on a file that is not shared by nature | Hides the boundaries instead of stating them |\n| Exporting a name | Moves the problem to `shrink`, or into the public API |\n| A name bent to carry the namespace | Passes the check and misleads the reader |\n| Regenerating the baseline over new findings | Records your new crossing as if it were old |\n| `//declscope:ignore` without a reason | The next reader cannot tell a decision from a shortcut |\n\n**Config changes are the repository owner's decision.** Ask before writing or changing one.\n\n## Traps\n\n**A package that does not compile is skipped, not checked.** declscope prints","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false,"persistedOutputPath":"/logs/agent/sessions/projects/-workspace/c2b8ba51-0db5-4d81-afe9-4988cb71a59c/tool-results/bmg252hgo.txt","persistedOutputSize":30670},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"toolu_01T5APogm1rygMtNu8QunR1B","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

A `//declscope:namespace` above the package clause names it instead.\n\n| Declaration | Scope by default | Who may use it |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Unexported | `private` | Its own namespace only |\n| Exported | `shared` | Any file of the package |\n| With `//declscope:shared`, or in a file with one above the package clause | `shared` | Any file of the package |\n| With `//declscope:private`, or in a file with one above the package clause | `private` | Its own namespace only |\n\n**A field or an interface method takes the nearest scope stated for it.** The order is its own directive, its type's, a file-level one, then the default. With nothing stated, an unexported field of an exported type is private.\n\nA method is not a member. {\n\tdir := m.pass.Pkg.Dir\n\tif dir == \"\" {\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\tseen := make(map[string]bool)\n\tfor _, f := range m.pass.Pkg.GoFiles {\n\t\tseen[f] = true\n\t}\n\tfor _, f := range problem(d *directive, msg string) {\n\tm.problems = append(m.problems, finding{\n\t\trule:    \"directive\",\n\t\tpos:     d.pos(),\n\t\tmessage: msg,\n\t\tdir:     d,\n\t})\n}\n\n// validate checks one directive and, if it is valid, records it at its\n// binding site.\nfunc (m *model) validate(f *fileInfo, d *directive) {\n\tswitch d.name {\n\tcase \"shared\", \"private\", \"ignore\", \"core\", \"namespace\":\n\tdefault:\n\t\tif d.fileLevel {\n\t\t\tm.problem(d, fmt.Sprintf(\"declscope:%s is not a file-level directive\", d.name))\n\t\t} else {\n\t\t\tm.problem(d, fmt.Sprintf(\"unknown declarations the rules check.\nfunc (m *model) collectDecls() {\n\tinfo := m.pass.TypesInfo\n\tadd := func(id *ast.Ident, kind string, f *fileInfo, t *target) *decl {\n\t\tif id == nil || id.Name == scopeSource) {\n\tlive := func(x *directive) bool { return x != nil && !skip[x] }\n\tt := d.target\n\tif live(t.scope) {\n\t\treturn t.scope.name, scopeSource{kind: srcOwn, dir: floats incl. `.inf`, `-.inf`, `.nan` → !!float; quoted scalars → !!str; explicit tags like `!!str`, `!!map` respected.
